i really despise supporting an organization that doesn't recognize the hard work and labor of their most important employees - the doctors and nurses. it's obvious that this hospital needs more staffing. it's also obvious that the current staff is amazing and has stepped up way beyond what they should to make sure the patients don't feel like the hospital is short staffed. this isn't their job. they deserve way more compensation than the idiotic upper management bureaucrats that have literally done nothing for patients while these nurses and doctors do everything. sorry not sorry to go off on a rant, but the nurses and doctors at this location are the only reason i keep coming back. the lack of integrity of this company and obvious lack of care for patients from their upper management makes me want to run screaming to any other hospital in the area. pay your nurses, hire more nurses, stop taking advantage of how amazing they are.

so i went in for a d&c, which is a fairly standard operation. no matter how i tried, i couldn't get them to put into their medical records that i'm allergic to some antibiotics--one severely. my primary care doctor told them. i believe my ob-gyn's office told them, but friday afternoon before i was to have surgery, they called me on an old phone number i haven't used for fifteen years (somehow, it still put a notice in my email), and when i called back, they had no record of these allergies. 

what they wanted (it was a nurse who didn't seem to care about putting in my drug allergies) was $4,000 upfront, or they wouldn't operate. i needed this operation to rule out cancer, so i argued them down to $1,000 upfront.

the medical information they had on me was 20 years out-of-date, including illnesses i hadn't had since my 20s. i'm almost 50. 

spooked by this horrible record-keeping, i made sure to walk in on the day of my operation with several printed copies of the medicines i was taking and the medicines i was allergic to. i gave these out to several nurses. (it was never clear to me who was a nurse and who was a med-tech. they should introduce themselves better.)

on intake, they mentioned that they gave people lavender essential oils as part of pain relief. i told them not to--that i was allergic. lavender gives me asthma. remember this....

so i gave out my sheet listing my medications and allergies to several people, but when i got into the operating room, one of the last things i remember the surgeon saying was, "so, no allergies?!" i told him then and then--they were already giving me things through my iv, that i had a severe reaction two two common antibiotics (clarithromycin and cirpo) and could not take them.

this was after telling seven people that i had these issues.

so i woke up in recovery, and there was the nurse, trying to give me lavender.

i told her to go away.

i was in pain, but only accepted an extra-strength tylenol because i was afraid that, if i was out-of-it, and they screwed up and tried to give me something that would make me sick, i wouldn't be able to stop them.

harbor hospital is not a safe place to go because they can't get basic info about your drug allergies into their system.

getting money out of you is more important than taking care of you.

having interviewed the ceo of bs&w-irving more than six years ago for an irving chamber of commerce video project, i've been curious about the impact of cindy schamp's vision and values on the "front lines."   where philosophy often gets punched in the nose by reality.  she impressed me as a remarkable leader - and i've interviewed many, including a u.s. surgeon general, presidents, and ceos. 

i had a forced opportunity to experience reality at bs&w-irving when i took my wife to the er a couple of days before christmas.  i was highly impressed by the care, expertise, teamwork, and professionalism of the entire team including the on-call surgeon ed clifford, md.  when we walked through the halls, staff members made eye contact, smiled, and said "hello."  when we needed to locate the cd with cat scan results we dropped off at the reception desk, the team member in charge of records made an exhaustive effort to locate it in the hospital like it contained precious images of a loved one.  and we were met with smiles from members of my wife's care team when she was cleared for release.  the image i grabbed says it all.

when i asked if they knew cindy schamp everyone gushed with how wonderful she was and the interest she showed in her people.  "we love it here" in the words of a nurse.  they were all impressed by the improvements she made -- from the new facility to the commitment to education.  the list is too long to post here.

maybe it was the christmas spirit.  and i can't promise all patients and visitors will see cindy schamp's vision come to life, but on this visit it did.  if you're curious about that vision, just google "cindy schamp grandma test" for one of her favorite stories on video, then watch a few dozen videos by googling for her name, then video.  learn  more about her winning values even if you're not ceo of a major medical facility.

that'll do, kaiser san leandro. it's always a pleasure for me to visit this facility. in the highly unlikely event i were to move back to the bay area, it would be an honor to practice medicine here, or any of the other kaiser offices. nonetheless, being a patient is more than fine by me, and when i'm next in town, i know where to go for my healthcare needs. until then!

i could not be more impressed or pleased with my experience at kaiser san leandro 1 week ago. i was admitted for a full right knee replacement surgery very early in the morning as i was asked to arrive at 6am for 8am surgery time. we had to drive over from marin county and needed to allow for any extra traffic delays. 

from the moment we went in through the emergency doors, there was something making me feel comfortable right away. the parking was so easy compared with the congestion and confusion experienced at the oakland facility where my surgeon is. from the get-go, every staff person we encountered were very helpful and so friendly. 

once we got to the surgery section, it was 100% care for the remainder of my stay that day until being discharged by 4:30 to head home. my surgical prep nurse was elizabeth, and wow, so thorough and a lot of patience with me. i knew i was in the hands of a very kind and well-prepared woman! she put me at ease and made my husband comfortable there too. 
then it was a hoot when i heard the anesthesiologist rolling down the hospital corridor on his stool and making the announcement,  "hi, i'm andy the anesthesiologist, and here to discuss how we will manage your pain" ! he carefully explained my options and cleared away my concerns about choosing a spinal. he took the time to go into my medical chart and clarify where having a spinal would be my best option and work within the parameters of my spinal stenosis issue in the lumbar region. he reviewed an mri from 2015 and said they would know how and where to administer that safely. big relief! great results on that. 

i couldn't have felt more comfortable with the 2 nurses on staff once i returned from surgery! they were ruben and destinie. i kept having difficulty recalling ruben's name but once he said, "like the sandwich, just call me mr. ruben sandwich" that finally sunk in. maybe it was the drugs! they were an awesome team!  they had their goals and kept me on track for an easy discharge. and they had such a terrific demeanor. 

of course, i got a visit from my surgeon, dr. eric eisemon, before we departed.  we first met at his office at kaiser oakland. he made me feel confident from the beginning that i would be in great hands with him doing my surgery and obviously he achieved the results he wanted! its now 1 week out and i am feeling really amazingly well and on my way to healing well! 

before i departed, i had 1 more visit from the anesthesiologist, 
dr. katragadda. he came to inquire whether he could put a catheter into my upper thigh  which would function for the next 4 days to slowly disperse a numbing med and keep me more comfy. he gave me the option and i selected it....so happy i made the decision to do so.  

as for the facility of kaiser san leandro ...i'm giving it *****.
..that's a 5-star rating!!  
1st of all: the parking
according to the 2 family members who needed to park, both said it was "super easy" and close to going into the hospital. the oakland kaiser is more like a zoo....impossible, time-consuming, and paying by the hour can get pricey. my family said it was free with excellent communication helping guide visitors where they needed to be and how to get there.

the hospital was well-laid out and organized. the best part: there was always a staff member to get help on finding where one needed to go.

but for me, i just loved that i was in a "state of the art" hospital. it was modern, so well-equipped. there was a sense of well-being there and a feeling that you were in very capable hands, not just going through the motions, but wanting one to thrive there!  the theme kaiser permanente strives for.  when my pt worker came to my home the next day for our first session, we talked a bit about my incision. i told him it seemed pretty sure that the scar that would remain would be much more minimal than the one in my left leg from the replacement surgery just 7 years ago when they used staples to close up my incision!  that old scar is not attractive at all. and then he told me that other kaiser facility still uses staples to close the wounds after surgery!  wow, san leandro seems light years ahead!!
i could not be more pleased with my decision to have had my surgery at kaiser san leandro!

i have a trained service dog for mobility and medical alert. while my disabilities can be invisible, it's usually not as you can see i have a major walking issue. i worked with a local service dog training organization that meets assistance dogs international standards to get him. he is legit, no amazon certificate or anything. he took 2 years of training and cost tens of thousands to train.

his mobility vest is made of leather. it doesn't fit currently (we think it shrank due to rain and not having proper care taken of it) and we're waiting on his new one to come in (takes up to 8 weeks because it had to be custom made as it's a mobility/guide vest). still, he was leashed to his collar and had a couple leash wraps that showed he was a working service dog. we even put on his working booties (they're heavier duty than what you can get at petco and meant for working dogs). we have the laws printed out and highlighted and i/my boyfriend both know how to answer the required questions.

yesterday, i had three important doctors appointments. i've waited several weeks for them (about a month) and they were supposed to be a new step in figuring out my chronic disability. they were also about a 40 minute drive to get to them. between the first appointment and the second, i thought it would be a good idea to get a printout of my medical records, as my new school was requesting them.

this meant going from the clinic side to the hospital side, where they had the hospital administration who dealt with these requests. while waiting to see someone, i noticed a bit of commotion going on but decided to focus on filling out the paperwork. i had noticed someone called the cops or security, but i was entirely oblivious to why. when i was called back i was told they would get my paperwork filed but i would need to leave as the cops has been called, so if i protested they would escort me out by force. this entire time, my dog hadn't even lifted his head from his nap, tucked beside my feet and out of the way. the administrator talking to me told me it was bs because she knew me and my dog and has seen him vested before, but they'd had five complaints about him (particularly his size) and so i'd need to go. the administrator confirmed it was due to his size/not being vested and that his behavior had been perfect.

i pulled up texas state law on my phone as well as the ada. they said it didn't matter as it was hospital policy. i left, unable to go to the rest of my appointments (missed ), obviously. they told me i wouldn't be welcome back to any of their hospitals or clinics until he was wearing his new vest (takes about 2 months to get). 

i called the head of hospital administration, michelle, to get a copy of the policy. she confirmed it and said by it saying she didn't care what i thought the law said. she refused to hear me out and kept talking over me any time i tried to say it was against the law. she also started talking about how my dog was unleashed and causing issues (wtf?!), which is completely untrue and i have several witnesses that can attest to that. even the doctor i saw earlier today told me she was afraid of dogs, especially big ones, but she was beyond impressed with how well behaved mine was. he was completely leashed and i can show you a picture of everything he was wearing yesterday.

to make this story even worse, this is the second time they've done something like this to me. the first was in the exact same department about 9 months ago. the greeter stood up as soon i walked in and screamed "get that thing the fuck out of here!" i spoke with hospital administration after that incident and they told me they had dealt with it and will provide better training for their employees and volunteers on service dogs.

with so much negativity in the media about various health care issues that it is easy to overlook those caregivers who do their best to provide the best possible care.

i have just finished six weeks of outpatient rehabilitation for a bi-lateral knee replacement at the rehab services department at broward health in coral springs. 
  
everything - from the warm and compassionate greeting from joanie who answered my initial, very  nervous call - to the sessions thrice, then twice, then single weekly sessions paul mcgowen have been noteworthy for his skill, compassion, encouragement  and knowledge of various physical therapeutic exercises.

understanding that i have made years of accommodations for my fused knees prior to my surgery, paul incorporated hip and lower back exercises into my pt plan.  he gave me exercises for home and followed up each session with a progress report.  he told me what to watch for - how to correct myself.  in short - he cared.

bhcs rehab consists of an incredible group of people - and for this, the program director, ms. pomerantz should be recognized.  she has put together an incredible team.  it was not unusual for any of the other therapists - edwin, amanda, allison and monica - to stop by me (either on the table or on a machine) to cheer me on.    youlanda was always ready provide heat and ice and tell me how great i was doing.

i have been to other facilities for physical therapy.  i know what it is to be treated as a case number.  i know what it is to be viewed as an insurance claim and nothing more.  this is not the case at broward health coral springs.  my experience with paul and his colleagues has completely "etch-a-sketched" those very negative experiences from my memory. 
 
my life has changed dramatically for the best - and i owe much of it to paul mcgowan and the rehab group at bhcs.  i thank them all.

hopefully you read this before going to the er, not after like i did.  reading some of the other reviews - similar things happened to me.

on friday february 28th at about 8:30pm my daughter and i took our 18 month old grandson to the emergency room on bee ridge and cattlemen.  

1.  my daughter was holding the baby who was crying - he had been bitten on the hand by a dog.
2.  the security guard never looked up from his computer and mumbled for us to sit down - "they know you're here."  we were the only people in the er, so i'm thinking "who knows we're here?"
3.  three women were behind a desk and did not make eye contact with us - no concern for a young woman holding a crying baby.  they just talked to each other - nobody told us anything.
4.  five minutes becomes 10 minutes and nobody said anything to us.
5.  after about 10-12 minutes a door marked triage opens and some patient comes out.  the triage nurse asked us to come in.
6.  she did not wash her hands, use purell, or wear gloves.
7.  she had to do all the typing to get us into the system (i guess the other three women were busy not helping)
8.  after about 15 questions - she finally asked why we were here.  we told her he had been bitten by a dog.
9.  when she reached for his hand - he of course screamed - so she reached for an unsanitized teddy bear on her desk and gave that to him to quiet him down.
10.  she dabbed the wound clean (did not rinse it) and moved us through some double doors into another waiting room with about six chairs - again we were the only people there.
11.  about another 10-15 minutes later a nurse came in and confirmed the baby's name.  then she asked us if he had a fever?  no?  a cough?  no?  we told her he had a dog bite.  (i wonder why she hadn't read the triage report??)
12.  she asked my daughter a dozen questions which had nothing to do with the dog bite, including vaginal or c-section delivery?  i'm guessing that is a priority when treating a dog bite.
13.  another 10 - 15 minutes and a doctor came into the room.  and here's where i started to question this whole operation.  he never came closer than 10 feet from the baby - never looked at the wound, let alone cleaned it.  from 10 feet away he then described what he was going to do - he was going to order an x-ray and then give us some antibiotics - because he told us without antibiotics the risk of infection is very high.
14.  another 10-15 minutes and a guy from x-ray came and told us he had been instructed to an x-ray of the right hand.  "is this _____?"  good guess!

did you ever see the movie zootpia where she has to go to the dmv to get her license?  that's what this experience brought to my mind.  they were like the sloths but without the smile and the compassion.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=drhsktakrzc 

15.  another 30 minutes and the nurse came back asking us what was happening.  that is when i got a little frustrated and asked her why the doctor had not even looked at the wound?  why hadn't the wound been cleaned?  she seemed to think that the doctor had looked at the wound.
16.  i could go on and on...

finally the nurse came back with the prescription for the antibiotic - it was now 11 at night.  i asked her if she could call in the prescription so it would be ready when we got there.  "we don't provide that service."

this is a perfect example of an organization which is driven by procedure - and has absolutely no focus on patients.  no compassion, no coordination, no communication.  the system these people work in has crushed their humanity - and this is with an empty er.

all the while i'm thinking to myself - "omg imagine if there was a corona virus outbreak in sarasota and there were five or six puking sick people in the er waiting room?  this hospital is completely unprepared to handle anything like that."

come to find out two days later that there was a corona virus patient in the hospital that night - and i thought back to the people not washing their hands, etc. etc.  i pray that my grandson, my daughter and i were not infected.  

and hannah b. don't respond "i am so sorry to hear about your experience..."  if you gave a damn, you would go to the er yourself and see what your customers see - it isn't pretty.  if you did care, it would either be fixed, or you wouldn't be working there.

i have been dealing with kaiser for a few years now because i am a caregiver to a family member with kaiser. i wish my family member did not choose kaiser.   like most businesses, it's hard to find good customer service or service nowadays.  there are a few "gems" who work at kaiser, but there are also a bunch of duds, from nurse aides to doctors to administrators. 

here are a few examples of the recent/past negative experiences (it's getting worse):  

1.  we had a cardiologist who went mia (he was here one day, and abruptly left back to the mainland...). there's more on this cardiologist....tmi      it's not easy to see a cardiologist--problems hiring/retaining.

how does one know this is a "verified" caller from kaiser asking for a credit card# over the phone?  see #4 how do i get on the "no call" list?

4. a family member with power of attorney cannot email kaiser on behalf of a family member's account, but has to "jump through hoops" to set up a (so called "verified") separate account to email kaiser on behalf of the family member.  yet, it's okay for doctors, nurses, social workers, patient coordinators to call/speak/meet with the family member with power of attorney.  yet it's okay for the fiscal office to call family member with power of attorney for payment...just not email. who's to say who we are via email, phone, or  in-person?!

as an almost 25 year military veteran who's been fortunate enough to serve around the globe, and been in quite a few hospitals and medical facilities.  this hospital is by far the worst i've ever encountered! earlier this month, i had the misfortune of visiting this hospital's er during a medical emergency of severe pain in my shoulder, arm, and fingers.

this review is for labor and delivery/maternity/triage

we arrived around 2am ish??? on sunday. the security helped us find a wheelchair and we were off to the second floor! the two front desk ladies were really accommodating and made it all as easy as possible for us to check in. insurance and all. i was wheeled to triage as soon as someone could come to get us and although i was in pain and it seemed as though time was going so slow, it was quicker than i thought it would be. but i was lucky enough that it wasn't busy at all that night. 

one of my biggest fears was waking my husband up in the middle of the night only to go and be told i wasn't dilated enough. so i waited until i just couldn't handle it anymore and i was 2.5 min at least in between contractions. everyone is different though so make sure to call ahead and ask to speak to a nurse. 

this isn't our normal hospital, nor have we been seen here ever so there was no record of our labs or anything. i was taken care of swiftly in triage. they were patient, kind and patient even though deep inside i felt pretty irritable being in pain. they tried to pull up some of my records but the system was down for the place i get my labs done at. they took all my test right then and there at triage. i was definitely in labor and they found me a room. 

the room was intimidating at first because all i could think of was "this is it! this is the place!" anyways, to keep this part short, i wasn't progressing and i was in so much pain so i was slowly induced and got the epidural. i pushed for a few minutes and bam. we had our baby and it was almost pain free compared to the contractions. the cramping and the stinging on the few stitches i got were far worse after the epidural was done. 

we were there long enough to see two shifts and they were both amazing. both doctors, all the nurses, even though i was getting kind of rude from not being able to eat while waiting to dilate all the way. (sorry everyone) it was amazing and i wouldn't have had the experience  anywhere else. 

recovery room, great. you get shown more than a few times on how to breastfeed your baby if you're there long enough which is nice in my opinion because i hate asking questions but they really make sure you can do it so you are a confident momma when you leave. you get the tools you need for using the restroom, and for when your baby uses the restroom. they even provided blankets and pillows for my husband and included him on everything. 

food:
hospital food always just rubbed me the wrong way and im not sure if it was truly good or if i was just so famished from starving and pushing lol, but i actually quite liked it believe it or not. and the menu is pretty accommodating especially if you are vegetarian or vegan. they have good options and your guests can go to the cafeteria and grab food there. my husband is pretty picky and he seemed to like it. there's also a subway there too. 

right after pushing, i got chicken tenders and fries with soup, salad, and ice cream. 

for breakfast i got cereal, eggs, and a muffin with coffee. 

dinner, i had a lot of options but i really wanted those chicken tenders again lol. but i also had the choice of teriyaki chicken and rice. 

she also took my order for the next morning and lunch to follow.

they always have the burgers and tenders on there if you don't want what they are making that day. 

they answer their call lights fast in my opinion and i've been to places that straight up just lag. but again, there are a lot of factors at play there so take that however you want. 

we would not have wanted to deliver anywhere else. i'm glad we came to pomona valley. my colleagues loved delivering here and i am glad we did too. amazing team they have here. thank you pvh

i was the support person for my daughter's recent labor and delivery. the labor and delivery service was mostly good, but the time after the delivery was awful.
we came to the delivery room around midnight and my daughter delivered at 2:30 with an uncomplicated natural childbirth with no pain medication. the delivery was very smooth and the dr. was skilled and personable. i thought it was a wonderful delivery.

because i was my daughter's support person, i was there for the entire 31 hours after delivery. and this is my story. 

we got in the recovery room about 4 and the nurses began their protocol of patient care. my daughter was not allowed to sleep more than 2 hours at a time, plus she was caring and feeding her newborn. nurses continued to wake her up over and over for some sort of patient care, that was in my opinion mostly unnecessary. at one point a nurse came in to wake her up and ask her if she wanted a pain pill. where is the common sense in that?
i got her out of there as quick as possible because she needed rest after being exhausted by delivery. she guesses she got 3 hours of sleep in the 31 hours she was there after delivery. perhaps this is a way to get new mothers out as soon as possible?

the sad thing is many new parents don't realize how abusive this protocol is and just accept it as normal. even the lactation specialist i complained to said she had her baby at home for that exact reason. a natural, un-medicated delivery is a normal part of life. and in my opinion the hospital's patient care is abusive.

we all joke that new parents are sleep deprived, but in the hours after delivery a new mother should be allowed to sleep if baby will let them. i worry about other mothers who may have had complication. they need the rest more than anyone and i know they will be denied rest by hospital patient care. 

we asked to be left alone for a few hours for sleep. the staff agreed then just continued on with all the things they are required to do. 

we left a day early so my daughter could come home and get some rest and she has been doing that. she would have liked to stay the full time because she has another child to care for and she is a single mother, but she told me she was so exhausted, that she needed to leave. she said she couldn't keep her eyes open and i saw that every time her eyes closed she would immediately be asleep. how is a person that exhausted able to care for a newborn or even herself?

i'm sorry for anyone who delivers at a hospital especially this one.  patients are trusting your hospital with their health and a very very important part of health is rest.

in feb 2019 i went to stanford for a small surgery for a hiatal hernia that started at 1:00 pm. i woke up from the surgery about 6pm in tremendous pain in my neck and shoulders.  they gave me something right away that helped me sleep, but wore off after a few hours. at 10:30pm, i woke up again in pain, i asked for more pain meds but was told i had to wait till 1am. by the time the night nurse showed up at 1:30 am, i was sobbing in pain and not able to move! at one point, they missed the vein and the pain meds created an egg sized bulge in my arm. ultimately the surgeon had me stay an extra day because my pain wasn't under control.

during the 2nd day the day nurses were wonderful, took very good care of me, they were responsive cheerful and i was always comfortable. i couldn't have asked for anything more.

however at night, it was a nightmare! the 2nd night i asked for the same pain meds as they gave me during the day, but they refused. even the charge nurse refused to give me pain meds and never called the attending. she seemed annoyed that i even asked. i had asked the night nurse  for a schedule of when i would get pain meds as i wanted to know if i had to last 1 hour in pain or 3 hours. she refused to tell me. the night nurse told me in front of the charge nurse if i was asleep, i was fine and she wouldn't wake me to give me pain meds.  the second night after surgery i went 8 hours with no pain meds at all. zero! needless to say, i crashed and ended up in severe pain the morning of the 3rd day.

when the attending dr. showed up the morning of the 3rd day, he told me if i needed any pain meds, just ask the nurse. i told him they weren't giving pain meds at night but during the day it was a different story. he checked the chart and his eyes got very big, he then made sure i was comfortable! i would have been better off going home the second day where i could have gotten care. i know it may sound like i am some kind of addict, but i actually don't like opioids and got off them as soon as i could. but they were a necessary part of being able to heal.  

if you go to have surgery, understand what the plan of care is, how the communication amongst the staff works, who is in charge of your plan of care, how to make a request if you need something and who your advocate is. i regret i didn't ask more questions. once i was in the hospital bed, i was treated like a non-person by the night nurses, an annoyance when i asked for help and dismissed when i was in pain. it was a terrifying experience to be so unable to take care of yourself and have the night nurse staff have total control of keeping you in pain or relieving your pain, and not have any recourse.

i read that women are often dismissed when they are in pain. i can sadly say that was the case for me at stanford, but only at night!

this review is for maternity care and child birth

on 26th december 2019, me and my husband were blessed with a baby girl at the stanford valley care hospital in dublin, ca. 

i was admitted to the hospital on the morning of 12/25/2019 when my water broke.

our daughter was born on 12/26/2019 in the afternoon. experience so far was good. we were discharged on 12/28/2019 in the afternoon around 1:00 pm only to return to emergency at 5:00 pm. that morning we had informed the staff that the baby is not fed almost the entire night. apart from not taking the feed, the baby was crying inconsolably all night. we called the staff multiple times, but nothing was done or taken care of. next day the lactation nurse helped us feed at about 11:00 am. the wait in the emergency room which was more that a couple of hours was very discomforting and causing more concerns. 

my concern is that we should not have been discharged, if the baby was not well. we were informed that the bilirubin levels of the baby were on the higher side. we asked the nurse what steps need to be taken for high bilirubin levels. however, the nurse said some kids have high level. all these days after the baby was born, we had been complaining that the baby is not feeding, to which the nurses and the doctors mentioned that it is normal since they are learning to latch. we had multiple times informed that the baby is constantly sleeping and not feeding. at this time, nobody provided us with the formula. when we returned to the emergency and the bilirubin test indicated that the levels are significantly very high and hence readmitted to the hospital. we learnt there that there was a misunderstanding that the baby was given the formula after birth, however that was never the case. 

we have faith in the hospital staff for discharging us, which makes us feel all is good with the mother and the baby, which was not in this case. we also noticed that the adjacent bed baby had a similar case, only thing is that they were discharged on 12/28/2019 and they came to back on 12/29/2019 morning. i believe, in such cases extending the stay and treating the baby will be better than the hassle of been discharged and then returning through emergency. 

this not only put us through a lot of discomfort and stress but also has financial implications. 

i would really appreciate if this can be looked into and not cause stress to other new parents.

!!do not bring your child here with asthma or difficulty breathing!!

team has little-to-no knowledge of pediatric pulmonology. my child has asthma that is triggered by chest colds and she had pneumonia (bad combo). 

she needed a strong steroid (which is usually the first step every time i've ever taken her to the er for asthma). instead of giving her a steroid treatment, the doctor on duty was convinced that my child needed to have a magnesium infusion. she was going to need the iv for being admitted anyway, so i consented. i was not informed of how painful these infusions are. my child was put through a painful, invasive magnesium infusion (which for some reason the whole staff was obsessed with doing) - which ended up doing absolutely nothing for my child. 

she was in constant pain from the iv, and they didn't once offer her any pain medication or any type of pain management (no heating pads, no nothing). the nurse practitioner was rude, harsh, had almost no bedside manner, and treated me like i had no clue what i was talking about. she literally said (in a sarcastic, clearly-feigning-empathy, tone) 'oooh, poor baby' to my child who was in pain and crying from the mag. treatment (which was completely unnecessary and ineffective). i've had a child with asthma for 8 years - i know what works - and the nurse practitioner treated me like an idiot and blew me off. 

i had to basically beg them to give her a steroid. they finally did, but not before telling me that she needed to be in the icu. i didn't think she needed to be in the icu (they were stating 'hospital policy' based on the fact that she needed hourly breathing treatments - which could be done in a regular room?? - not making the decision based on the severity of her asthma) - she wasn't in distress, she was calm, she just needed breathing treatments because her o2 levels were staying low. (pro tip: constant albuterol treatments will lower your o2 levels - the staff didn't seem to know this) they didn't have any available rooms in the icu (probably because their standards for admitting someone to the icu are so low), so they basically insisted we be moved via ambulance to dell children's. 

this was probably the only thing that st. david's did right. the dell team showed up - took one look at my child - and said "she doesn't need to be in the icu". when we got to dell - one of the first questions they asked was 'has she had a steroid yet' - wow, what do you know - mom knew what she was talking about! they also told me not to worry too much about her o2 levels - which st. david were obsessed with - because, as stated above, constant albuterol treatments will lower your o2. at dell they immediately took her off of oxygen, gave her additional steroids, moved her breathing treatments from every hour to every 3 hours, she was able to cough a bunch of stuff up, and we were able to go home the next day.

save yourself the trouble and stress and bring your kids to dell children's for asthma (or anything else for that matter). they have extensive pediatric pulmonology knowledge (a whole wing dedicated to it!), they treated me like a person, considered and listened to my opinions, gave a sh*t when my child was in pain, and their team made me feel so at ease after the hell that was st. david's north austin. 

i will never bring my child to another st. david's. i will always go straight to dell.

i feel bad giving hospitals bad reviews, but this time, it's necessary. i brought my son in with severe back pain and sciatic leg pain. we got here at 2:15. got into a room at about 3:00. a nurse came in and asked all the usual questions and said "ryan" (pa) would be in to talk to my son. one hour goes by. no one.  nothing for the pain. it's about 4pm and my son hadn't eaten anything. i went out to the nurse's station and asked if i could get something from the cafeteria for him. 'nurse one' says probably, but he needs to be seen by ryan to get the ok. i go back to his room and we wait. another hour goes by. i return to the desk and ask, "when will ryan go to my son's room?" 

nurse one - oh, he hasn't been in yet? i'll get him in there.

ten minutes later, ryan shows up, asks my son what's happening and he tells him about the severe sciatic pain and low back pain. 

ryan says, "so, what do you want us to do for you?" 

i'm shocked. he says,  well we can give you muscle relaxers. or, i guess we could do an mri." um, yeah. thanks, we'll take the mri.  and something for his pain right now? thanks....

i went to get my son something to eat and someone came in and gave him a shot of valium. valium? he's not having a panic attack... his disc is blown! 


we wait.

we wait. 5:30 a different nurse comes in and says they'll be taking him out for his mri soon - remove all metal etc. at 5:40, ryan comes back in and says, "well, its gonna be another couple hours until we can get you the mri, so if you want to go home, i can give you a prescription... you probably won't get the mri till 8 or 9."

at first, i'm like, yeah, we're going home this is bs. we'll  just go home and try to make it through the weekend. then i started to think about that.  if we went home, we'd go through the wind with him in pain. monday, try to get an appt with a surgeon. prob won't get an appt for that week. meanwhile, we still can't get an mri because we haven't seen a dr. to authorize it. weeks will go by without any help. 

so, i go back out and tell ryan we want the mri after all. he says he just cancelled it. i said reschedule.  

in less than 10 minutes, someone comes in to take my son to get the mri. really. 

i'm figuring ryan was trying to clear out the room my son is in without doing anything for him. its friday night and they need the room. 

this kind if care is what i'd expect with socialized medicine.  this is unacceptable.  i'd give a zero if i could. no attention, no urgency. they act as if severe pain shouldn't be an er visit,  make you wait long enough and maybe you'll just go home!!

we wait.

i have mixed feelings about my recent hospital visit. i'll start by saying that i first presented to the ed on 12/3 for a kidney stone. my ed visit went pretty quickly and i felt well taken care of. however, my pain didn't go away and during the night of 12/6 i returned to the ed. my original ct scan had showed a 3mm kidney stone and my us at the second visit showed a 6mm stone in the same location. so i feel like something was measured incorrectly there and i likely shouldn't have been sent home to pass a stone that large. i hope that someone is considering investigating this.

in any event, they offered me admission and consultation with a urologist, which i agreed to. i do understand that with flu season and snow birds coming into town census was very high. it took a very long time for me to get assigned a bed. when i finally did get a bed it was an overflow bed. what that means is that it was a bed in a hallway with a small partition in front of it. the lights in that area didn't turn off. the bathroom was a very long walk away for a patient with a urinary tract issue. needless to say i got no sleep. no one really explained to me that i would be going to an overflow bed...i just felt like there was a general lack of communication once i left the ed and was on the floor. it took the floor nurse a long time to get pain meds for me because they were apparently ordered for ed and not the floor and that was really challenging for me. i understand that this may not be the nurses fault, but i shouldn't have to suffer while they get it sorted. someone, maybe an administrator, came by early in the morning and promised to get me a room "sometime" but that didn't really happen.

i was fortunate that urology was able to fit me into their schedule later in the day friday and i had a procedure done. everyone in surgery was amazing. they explained everything and answered questions and kept me really informed. it took a while to get me out of recovery because, according to the observation unit, someone would assign me a bed and take me out, then assign me again...so she was surprised when i actually showed up. 

my night nurse, julie, on the observation unit was amazing. she was super attentive to my needs and helped me make decisions about pain control. i wasn't as jazzed with my day nurse, hayes. it seemed like she didn't believe my pain level. i felt like dr. khan, who discharged me, also felt that way. i asked her about pain meds at home and she told me i already had them filled on tuesday and if i needed more i needed to talk to my primary care doc. the ed had given me a small prescription of pain meds that i'd been taking for 3 days, so i only had a couple left. it was saturday and i was worried about just getting through to monday. she snidely said to me, "you do understand this is only going to get better, right?" then she was gone and i never saw her again. of course i knew the pain would be getting better, but i didn't want to be in a situation where my pain wasn't controlled over the weekend and i had to visit the ed again. luckily, the urologist had ordered some pain meds for me on discharge. 

overall i would say my biggest complaint was the care didn't seem super coordinated. after the doctor said she was discharging me hayes said she'd get the paperwork ready so i called my husband. after we'd sat there for quite a while i asked her about a couple things and then she's like, "oh, are you ready to go home?" like she was surprised by this? i thought we'd been waiting on her to bring us discharge papers. the discharge papers were 43 pages of notes about my condition and medication, but very little useful info regarding my actual stay. i guess i thought i might have gotten a care summary or something so that when i talked to my pcp i could speak to everything that had occurred.

so was it the worst hospital experience i've ever had? no. but was it the best? also no. would i recommend it to a friend? if it was an emergency, sure. but if you had choice in care...maybe not.

first and foremost, nothing but the utmost respect for all of the nurses and dr. tsai in the labor and delivery ward. they were pro's and honoring of the birth process. 

however... things took an abrupt and horrifying turn after our baby was born when the hospital pediatrician began the initial examination of our son and made several alarming observations and "diagnoses" that were not accurate. the false observations included:

1. a supposed heart murmur that warranted a 48 hour extended hospital stay.  4 additional heart auscultations by 2 different doctors and 2 nurses did not pick up any said murmur.

2. a supposed mild spinal bifida - non-union or closure of bones near the sacrum/buttocks (that was actually just a cute butt)  

3. supposed extremely low body weight and size- our boy was actually 6 lb 6oz and 19 inches long. just a small little guy.

4. said he felt hot and might have an infection. for the post birth examination, babies are placed under a heat lamp that if you are standing close by to it, feels like a nice warm outdoor heat lamp. i was watching his skin turn pink from the heat.... to be expected...and since i was able to assist in the delivery by catching him with the dr. and then placing him on my wife... i was well aware of his temperature as well as texture of the skin.

after the doctor's confusing and fear based examination we were asked if we wanted several other tests to be performed. since our boy possessed normal reflexes, had healthy muscular tone, skin color was normal (actually red from the heat lamp), we declined the optional tests that were recommended by this doctor ( i will update the accurate name later) because we did not trust her. she questioned us repeatedly on why we did not want the test and gave her informed answers knowing of the risks and benefits.... after all, both my wife and i are health care practitioners, and had done our research on the proposed tests. since there was no real indication to perform the "recommended" we declined. this doctor was so aggressive we wanted to leave the hospital immediately. we did not feel safe.

we were next transferred to the postpartum room where we encountered another warm and compassionate nurse who tended to our baby... who also said she heard no murmur.... only to be attacked by another pediatrician who wanted to do more invasive testing involved in the newborn screening. we declined the test which requires a slicing of the heel and milking of blood to assess for possible conditions. since my wife an i had already done our own blood work and had  blood work drawn while she was pregnant, that reveal zero genetic abnormalities.

we had two separate experiences... one with the ob/gyn and nurses involved in the actual birth and another one were we felt like we were in germany in the 1940's with aggressive and hostile doctors.

we wish we could share a more positive experience, but this was a huge stain on our experience. 

finally, to avoid this traumatizing situation, make sure your pediatrician has hospital privileges at ucla to examine your newborn or you will be subject to receiving an exam from the hospital pediatrician who may scare the heck out of you by saying something is wrong with your child. if your pediatrician does not have privileges, then make sure you find a trusted md that can come to the hospital. that's the best advice i can give you.

i finish my ct scan of my lungs and the tech comes out and says to me "we've just gotten off the phone with your doctor and he wants you to go immediately to mountain view hospital er"; you've got a pulmonary embolism in your lower left lobe.

so, i arrive at mv er and the team immediately takes me in, runs an ekg, takes blood, and performs an xray of my lungs; i was never alone.  because all er's are flooded with patients it doesn't surprise me to find myself rolled to an "easy chair" in the hallway of the er where i have to wait for a room to open up in the hospital.  3 hours later.... after being checked on frequently, they roll me into 5014 --- single room, huge, even has a couch that folds down to a twin so that my wife, if she had wanted to, could have spent the night!  surperb staff !  friendly, concerned, attentive, and helpful.  i spent the next few nights in 5014, getting my iv heparin, frequent vital checks, blood testing to check the heparin balances.  food, did i mention that they have great food delivery?  you order from a pretty wide menu (appropriate food for why you are there, of course) but you order, they deliver within 45 minutes of your order (usually sooner).  wow.

i was there for my birthday... my day nurse made up a birthday card for me.  everyone was super sweet and caring.  my wife and i were blown away.  of course, if it takes 3 hours to get in.... yup, on discharge day i told me wife we would not leave until 3pm.... okay, we got out by 2:55pm.  overall, wonderful experience during march when the hospital is being slammed with all the usual... plus.... flu... plus corona virus worriers coming in for checkups who are "healthy"...

thanks mountain view !
martin swartout

ps
  for those who have bad experiences with the er; consider that the er must triage all cases.... based upon life threatening need.  i remember 1965, my mother was so upset (livid) that i was still laying in a gurney in the er hallway back in california after a car drove through me on my bike.... six hours later... but then, on that friday night holy cross was having to deal with huge numbers of life threatening cases due to a large gang fight where knives, chains, clubs, and the like had caused a lot of mayhem.  we all feel that our's is the most important misery, that's natural, and it is important for each of us to have an advocate insuring that we aren't ignored or forgotten... but, bottom line, the er must triage.   blessings to you all, forgive me my brief lecture.

i'm done with st francis.  my husband has been to the er and admitted twice in the past 3 weeks.  yes  there are some good people there;  i can count about 7.  however,  overall it is clear that they are a hospital that hates people. 

 this is extremely problematic because they treat every patient as a huge inconvenience.  if you don't have an advocate you're in even more trouble.  i've watched them push around people and they are dismissive in general but are especially patronizing and condescending to older people and people whose first language is not english

 staff do not like to answer questions, and prefer if the patients just do what they are told and whatever you do, don't ring the call bell! if your medication is late, too bad.
 
 my husband's treatment and medications were routinely incorrect and at shift change it appeared that there were no handoffs nor did the next shift even read charts.  i think his treatment was drawn out longer than necessary because of the incompetence.  it would also get worse when you would point out the error and prove them wrong.

 we've both had rns lie to our faces.  when we called them out on something, they would just stand there and lie about something that had occurred 30 seconds before.  that shows a complete disdain for the patient, to think that they can behave badly, lie bald-faced about it and think we will just take it.

 of course, we didn't.  i work in healthcare and am my husband's advocate which was a huge irritant to them.  we pushed back, we questioned everything (they leave you no choice) we proved them wrong on multiple occasions and we called them on every lie. 

 the favored tactic of the staff when you're not being a "good sport" is to turn their back to you and ignore you.  the second favorite is to scream at you.  that's why an advocate is important, the only time they screamed at my husband was when i wasn't around.  and by the way, screaming is not an exaggeration. 

 of course the terrible behavior of the staff is reflective of the culture.  bad behavior starts at the top.  i would imagine that the upper levels are very unpleasant and likely incompetent.  here's the thing; good managers hire people that are smarter than them and trust them to do their jobs without micromanaging but also without being withdrawn.  bad managers, without fail, hire people who are no better or smarter and they prefer people they consider to be lessor than they.  they treat their employees as badly as their customers. the latter is an excellent example of what is going on at st francis.

normally, because of where we live, and our insurance,  st francis is nothing more than an er for us.  but these past two instances we had no choice, our contracted hospitals were full.  at this point in time, barring a full-scale,  life-threatening emergency, i'll strongly consider whether or not we can take the chance of going to tacoma or seattle.

 i cannot recommend st francis at all.  i feel badly for the people who have no other choice.  you may get lucky and get one of the few good nurses or doctors or pharmacists: but generally you will be treated as less than human, lied to, ignored, screamed at, and your overall treatment will be subpar.   i am truly embarrassed to work in the same field.

please, learn from my mistake. if you find yourself in an ambulance with an emt asking you which hospital to go to, under no circumstances say "king's county". say no to this place like your life depends on it. 

my particular horror story happened on a saturday morning when i began feeling a crippling, agonizing and debilitating pain in my abdomen, getting worse and worse. unable to move and barely able to stay conscious, i called 911 and an ambulance took me to the nearest hospital -- king's county. 

i was wheeled into the er on a gurney, crying and screaming in agony. after several minutes, someone asked for my insurance card. thinking that i was about to die, i cried and used profanity to plead for help. she said she didn't like my language and simply walked away.

i lay there, crying in agony and fearful that i was on death's door. i thrashed on my gurney, pleading for help. a full hour went by as i cried and pleaded for help, while the staff all around completely ignored me. i listened through my pain as they gossiped, engaged in long discussions about what they would have for lunch, and as they answered phones from people in distress and then joked about how "stupid" the callers were. after an hour a doctor happened to walk by. i reached out for him, pleading for help. he took one look at me and shouted at the staff that i should be a priority patient. 

i lay in the lobby for another 20 minutes, feet away from the open door in the middle of winter. 

finally i was wheeled into the hospital by a staff member who slammed my gurney into each and every door and wall, furthering the worst agony i had ever experienced. he ignored me, stopping to have a casual chat with another staffer about the upcoming super bowl. he then wheeled me into the middle of a busy hallway in the er, locked the wheels of the gurney, and left me there. for the next half hour, countless people bumped into me as my cries for help went unanswered. after vomiting several times, the pain became so unbearable that i lost consciousness. 

i woke up to a woman asking for my insurance again. i begged her for help, and she just walked away. 30 minutes later a friendly doctor (the only positive part of this experience) briefly examined me in the hallway (where privacy was nonexistent) and said they needed to run tests. after an endless wait, a horrendously mean nurse withdrew 5 vials of blood from my arm (i was later told this was a mistake and they only needed 2, so the others were disposed of). she hooked me up to an iv, left a bunch of literal garbage (wrappers and packaging from needles, etc) on top of me, and left. for 2 hours, no one would acknowledge my presence as i cried in pain. my questions went unanswered. it had been hours since i had anything to drink or gone to the bathroom, and with an empty iv bag connected to my arm, i was literally trapped on the bed, unable to move. 

i asked everyone who walked past (or rather, everyone who bumped into me) but i was ignored. occasionally, a nurse or staff member would walk by and treat me with about as much respect as they would give a stray animal. the staff here have no business dealing with patients, let alone other human beings. interacting with them was undoubtedly the single most dehumanizing experience of my entire life. 

after hours of this agony, of being ignored, of being literally denied the ability the use the bathroom or access to water, i told a staff member that i was on the verge of calling the police to report that i was being held captive against my will and tortured. this got their attention. the doctor came back, surprised that no one had spoken to me, surprised that i had been tied to this bed for so long, and very surprised that the nurse dumped her garbage on top of my lap. she ordered more tests and unhooked my iv. i waited 17 minutes to use the only available bathroom, peed into a cup, and held onto the urine for another 30 minutes until someone took it. after another endless wait, she came back to say she thought i had a kidney stone and suggesting i get a ct scan. well i finally got that scan, but they didn't bother to walk me back to my bed so i got lost, wandering the sprawling hospital halls... 

after a full day of being abused, abandoned, restrained, ignored, and borderline tortured, i wad diagnosed with a kidney stone, given a prescription to pick up from a pharmacy that had already closed, and sent on my way. look, no er is a fun place, and i understand that this one is working under exceptionally difficult circumstances out of their control. but there is simply no justification for what i experienced. i once visited a hospital in an impoverished, rural community in china, and the people there were treated with infinitely more respect and dignity. king's county er resembles a hospital from a post-apocalyptic zombie movie. but in a world without zombies, there is simply no excuse. shame on them. shame! you've been warned.

this review is regarding the in-patient general hospitalization-not the er which is where our visit started. since i am usually a positive person, i'll start with the positive:
     every single staff member from the receptionist to the triage nurse to the er nurse to the er dr's to the transporters were so incredibly sweet and attentive. the er entrance is tiny and overwhelmed with people. inside is the same way. so in spite of the terrible design, lack of space, and the overwhelming number of patients the er has, everyone handled themselves with such grace and treated the patients with such care. as stressed as their er employees must be by the sheer volume of cases they handle daily/nightly, everyone we met seemed to keep a great attitude and a calm demeanor. 

now, to the in-patient part,  wow! was this the same hospital?! that was my thought. in reading through previous yelp reviews, my family & i experienced the exact same discharge issues as others have. this is highly disturbing and worrisome. there needs to be a state investigation into their practices because i am sure that some would not hold up to the state law. i am going to actually file a complaint with the hospital and medical board. the main issues:
-incorrect diagnosis/follow up instructions on discharge paperwork. paperwork completed incorrectly/altered to make it look like the patient is ready to go home. in fact the nurse's & dr's attitudes made it terribly clear that they wanted my family member out asap so they could make space for their afternoon admits.
-both nurse and dr completely ignored my repeated statements that my family member's current health problems developed only following a fall and that this was actually what motivated the er to admit this person in the first place! what did the dr say, "he'll get a walker and a diaper. he's going home" in response to my request that the specialist that was called in the a.m. be fully informed of the symptoms my family member was experiencing. yes, my family member was released unable to get out of bed, unable to walk without assistance, & with additional concerning medical issues. we were told to wait for home hospital to call us in 24-48 hours. thank god that my family member has family who can step up and do the caregiving needed. imagine the person released who has not any family and is not able to lift themselves out of bed and cannot walk??!

-what happened when i asked them to correct their paperwork so we could use the paperwork as instructed? the case manager/nurse waved me off and told me i would have to request complete medical records downstairs. it was my first experience having to go in search of papers showing the correct diagnosis and follow up recommendations! 

-nurse gave incorrect instructions on otc meds dr prescribed. thank god again that i carefully read the discharge papers to find out that the med did not need to be taken as the nurse stated!!

-nurse was visibly stressed, wanted her lunch break before p.m. admits (stated this) & in a hurry with discharge paperwork so she ended throwing med bottles at my family member's feet as she attempted to correctly document the medication. at one point she was kind enough to ask, "did i hit you?" she kept having to come back because she couldn't get the meds written down despite having been given a list and the actual bottles. 

-nurse never put orders in for food for my family member after his emergency surgery was cancelled at 9am. my family member received no breakfast and no lunch. by 3pm, i finally requested lunch for him! 

-we were told we'd be talking with a social worker/case manager. that person never came and when i went to ask, a person shrugged and said they were a case manager but would not be talking to us. we were again told just go home and wait for a call from home hospital in 24-48 hours then waved off. 

if you or your family member want a hospital who makes mistakes, doesn't listen correctly to patients, & discharges people in such a haphazard and unorganized manner (i mean even the nurse's assistant forgot to dress my family member before leaving for the day and the stressed nurse made this clear to us!! i had to ask for my family member to be dressed!), then this may be the hospital for you. they are clearly looking at profit over patient care but it's to the point where you may be released in a worse state than in which you arrived and you may even be given incorrect instructions and reports. you may be, in some ways, worse off than before you were admitted. having strong family support is a must in case you need to come here. otherwise, steer clear for your health's sake.

i had a good experience at this er. 
i came in on a thursday at around 1pm with really awful pains in my chest and upper left shoulder/back and there was no one else in the waiting room. i immediately got checked in by the initial info. taker and looked at by the first nurse who checked my basic markers like blood pressure, temperature, reason for coming in, etc. he told me to take a seat and that they'd call me in "if they had room". which was a little worrisome, but i actually only waited for about 15 minutes or so before i got called in. 
i was taken to a private room by one nurse, met by another, and got changed into a robe, and started the process for my specific issue. the nurse we met in there was really rushing (the other nurse even pointed it out) - not even leaving the room to let me change into the robe - just holding it up and telling me to take off my clothes behind it - and asking me questions super quickly without even waiting for my response. i'm thinking and hoping that she just had something urgent to get to, because it was a little unnecessary, but nothing terribly awful. i took my time and made sure to get all my answers out before moving on. the other nurse was very kind asking if i wanted a warm blanket, etc. they were out the door in about 5 min after i got in. it took around 45 min or so before the dr. came in. 
he was really great. dr. mccall is his name. great bedside manner: calm, kind, allowed me to ask all of my questions and say all that i wanted to say. he took the time to thoroughly explain the results of the tests the nurses took, going into more detail about how to read it and what certain markers would and could mean, etc. he did a physical examination, as well, and explained everything as he went. explaining why i was probably feeling the way that i felt and what would cause it. i didn't feel rushed with him, and i felt like a person.

i was in and out of the building in about 2 hours!
and, parking is in a parking garage next door that was free (gate was open and there were no tickets) the day that i went.

i will have to see how billing goes, but in-person care was pretty good and thankfully much better than other reviewers' on here.

i can't imagine any other business where you are spending thousands of dollars at an establishment and the people working there treat the clients like they are trash, and are annoyed with them for existing.

i met the doctor for the first time during my stay in the er when he burst into the room saying, "i'd like to know what possible reason you could have for holding up a ct scan!"  not, "hello, how are you feeling?" not, "hi i'm dr. gionis."  i'd been waiting literally hours to see him the middle of the night, after a day spent throwing up with a fever. it was 3am.  i deserved kindness and gentleness, not being attacked.  that is an incredibly rude way to treat anyone, period. second of all, when you're the doctor and a large tall man, and your patient is a young woman, alone in the room, who is so sick she can barely speak, it's absolutely unacceptable.  

i was able to articulate to him that i had wanted to see the results of my bloodwork before further testing.  i have been in the er many times in my life for various issues including gastric related ones, and i have never had anyone order extensive imaging before even examining me.  this clinic ordered an x-ray and ct scan, in addition to a urine sample, blood panel, and other tests,  before anyone had even examined me!! i had no unusual symptoms of any kind and in all my er experiences, the imaging comes when something shows up in bloodwork or due to symptoms noted in the exam with the doctor.  they claimed they needed imaging to see if it was appendicitis or other internal organ issue.  yet no one had even palpated my  abdomen to check for localized tenderness.  so i felt like this was a racket and i had every right to request to be seen, examined, and to know if any results in my tests indicated the need for imaging.  they had already swooped in and x-rayed my lungs and i didn't even have a cough or any symptoms remotely related.  

i was there because i needed intravenous fluids and anti-nausea meds so i could rehydrate and take tylenol, get my fever down, and be well enough to drive the next day.  i was of course willing to be examined and appreciated them looking for signs of something other than food poisoning or the flu, but this was excessive and i had every right to question them and to want to talk to the doctor about why the hell a ct scan was being ordered before anyone had talked to me. 

when my mom and i questioned them on all the testing and why we weren't being seen by a doctor, we were treated horribly.  we were gaslit, and shamed.  they then kept me there for 5.5 hours, 12-5:30am, citing being a small clinic in a rural area.  it was a monday night in the off season.  there were one or two other patients the whole time i was there and yet we went hours without being spoken to or seen. and when my mom tried to get someone's attention, to get me a blanket, or some ice chips, or any info on when we might be seen, she was told she was violating hippa laws.  by walking outside the doorway.  

anyway, this place is awful.

i spent five hours here the other night.  i'd been awake for 22 hours when i left.  i hadn't taken my meds.  i was almost late for an appointment with my primary care physician after leaving.

the only reason i came back here was because it's the closest hospital to my house.  it's three times the distance to any other 24 hour facility.  (and they all have pretty poor reviews.)

the only reason it didn't take longer was because i asked to speak to a hospital administrator after sitting in the er waiting room for four hours.  we'd been there long enough for a staff rotation and the lady at the front desk said it would probably be two more hours before we'd be taken back at that point.

to be fair, triage occurred fairly rapidly after we arrived.  and they had done a blood draw and urine sample and running labs during the four hours we were sitting in the waiting room.  i was however told when we finally got taken back to a chair with a curtain around it that the labs had been completed 45 minutes prior.

the chairs are pretty uncomfortable.  the vending machine was broken.  the tv was playing the kardashians and that made me want to leave on principle.  i wish they were better at communicating status.  i am much more patient when i have an eta that updates.  but this place is purgatory.

i also realize that people get prioritized by need in the er, but it's super annoying watching people come in after you, get treated, and leave before you even leave the waiting room.  especially when you can hear the nurse tell them they just have the flu.

the hospital is recently new.  the facility is immaculate.  the staff is personable and many are very compassionate.  the food trays are excellent and have a good variety.  guest trays are reasonably priced.  a pullout bed is available for spouses or caregivers to stay overnight.  parking is a bit of a challenge due to the number of people being served.  usually, the doctors are tops. however, i doubt that i will ever go there for care in the future.  they are clearly understaffed.  

example #1:   my wife has a bladder problem.   she had just come out of knee replacement surgery.  about 3 hours later, she wet the bed because the nurse or aide did not answer the call in a reasonable time.  other calls were made.  my wife told me that she laid in her own urine from 7:00 pm to nearly 7:00 am.  it appears that the night shift may have had too much to do.

example #2:  one of the doctors decided that she was getting too much pain medication.  without contacting the surgeon who prescribed it, the doctor adjusted (reduced) the medicine to fit his wishes.   my wife subsequently complained of severe pain.  after over an hour of intense pain (she said the pain was a 12 on a scale of 1 to 10) she was finally told that a nurse would be in in about 20 minutes.  prior to that she had also called because she was wet again.  it was about an hour and a half before she received additional pain medication and about two hours of laying in her own urine again before they came and took her to the bathroom.

example #3  while i was taking my wife's suitcase to the car, the discharge papers were being given to my wife without my presence even though i would be the caretaker for the next few weeks.    when we got home and i started reviewing the information, the names of the  drugs on the paperwork didn't even match those on the pill bottles, and the amounts were duplicated.  i literally had to write down the scripts of ten different bottles and their bottle directions so i would know what and when to give.  

example #4:  as stated above, pain did not seem to be an issue for the staff.  upon discharge, my wife was taken to my car in a wheel chair.  as soon as she was pushed to the car, the attendant left.  my wife was in so much pain and so stiff from the bandages and surgery that she was nearly unable to get into the car.  we had to have her scoot herself along the back seat with me on the other side of the back seat helping to pull her in before we could even get the doors closed...all this without anyone from the hospital staff helping.  i almost took her to back to the hospital to be readmitted as she was in so much pain that it appeared that i would not be able to  accommodate her needs.  it was about four hours later after giving her the drugs that should have been administered in  the hospital that my wife was finally relieved of much of her pain.

i started by saying that the staff is compassionate.  when someone finally did come to my wife's aid, they were very kind and willing to assist.  so was the staff guilty of  incompetence?  doubtful?  lack of staffing?  likely.
one more note.  after my wife had laid in urine for an hour and a half without assistance, i arrived in the hospital and went into the hallway to solicit help since the pager on the bed was soliciting no response.  two women (nurses or nurses aids) were sitting together talking to one another right outside of my wife's room.  one did tell me that she would get a nurse, and she also helped take my wife to the restroom and clean the bed.  but why did it take an advocate to get help?

iu claims that newsweek has given them a top ten rating for hospitals.  my experience with the care given to my wife would say the bottom ten.

for the insane cost of this "private" facility, you'll end up in a whole world of hurt.

a close family member ("cc") was involved with this program for a little over 2.5 years. after "graduating," cc then relocated and continued in outpatient therapy with the same psychiatrist. a few months ago, we terminated treatment with this provider. we finally realized that the provider was squirrely at best and only sought to make messes for cc that he would have no part in cleaning up.

prior to entering treatment, cc was on zero medications, had zero hospitalization, and zero history of drug abuse. cc was in school full time, working part time, active in our church community, and generally managing. following a traumatic life event, we voluntarily chose to have cc enter the retreat on the recommendation of our home psychologist.

after a series of:
-tms (junk science),
-ect (victorian, invasive shock therapy),
-2 years worth of toxic medication trials, and
-1.5 years of outpatient group therapy
-relocating cc several states away to continue treatment,
we are at a massive loss emotionally and financially.

the retreat psychiatrist (who led our family member's care) had far too much faith in his own capabilities. he had a deceptively closed-minded focus on his personal field of study, which we know now, doesn't really help with the functional treatment of complex trauma. we didn't get to choose cc's providers, but knowing what we know now, we never would have chosen this path for them.

you practically need a phd in psychiatric practice to understand how this program works. we were very blindsided to learn that the arcane psychoanalysis was the foundation for the retreat's programming. they tout dbt, but it's two sessions per week, which are confusing and disorganized at best.

the treatment team routinely exercised poor judgement in assessing the dynamics of cc's complicated trauma background, which continued throughout the entire course of care. they essentially allowed cc's biological parents (and main payors) to dictate the care and treatment strategies used, which resulted in a series of misdiagnoses.

it's a rampant issue in healthcare, but the providers are wholly protected by the system from bearing any consequence for their "firm suggestions." they put the onus on the patients and their families to be the ultimate deciders, but it really became a toxic cycle of the blind leading the blind. we didn't feel like we had a choice at any point if we wanted cc to get on a path to recovery.

think of sinking an average year's salary for a 3-week-long diagnostic workup by a supposed "team of experts." a mix of art therapists and social workers will work with your psychiatrist to strong arm the patient into a desire to "get better" and then coerce the family into refinancing their home to get the recommended weeks to months of extended care at over $2000 per day. this includes an intensive regimen of loosey-goosey therapy groups, bizarre binders full of self-help jargon, and patient-guided group therapy. they are trying to be progressive, but it's a classic case of poor administrative controls and defaulting into letting the inmates run the asylum. it honestly feels like some of the providers get a kick out making things messy and watching us drown while we try to clean up catastrophe after catastrophe. they just smile at us and placate us with politicized psychiatric jargon.

once we pursued outside consultation, we realized we'd been completely, wholly, massively duped by these supposed "experts" and gamed by a very unregulated rehabilitation system. unless medication management and positive talk therapy are the $200,000+ boost you need, these people constantly come up short.

after all is said and done, we were dealing with an entirely different medical and psychiatric picture than the providers were willing to treat or even investigate. hundreds of thousands of dollars later, and hundreds of hours of travel, family therapy, and the many years cc devoted to their own therapy, we have very little to show for it.

we are left with immeasurable pain and suffering, a heap of debt, and a solid education in the toxic dysfunction of the behavioral health system.

came to this kaiser panorama city pharmacy for an emergency medication written by my pcp. thankfully, i looked at my member benefits and it said no charge for this medication. however, when i went to check out i was informed by the pharm tech that i need to pay retail price for it because she said it's not emergency and that routine medications are consider emergency. uhh, no sweetie, when the medication has the word "emergency" on it, it's considered emergency and medication you take every day to prevent something is not considered emergency. kaiser really need to look at education when hiring their pharmacy tech. anyways i told her to bill it to me. she said she can't do that. she finally had to ask someone else. thankfully a pharmacist who understand kaiser's policy, acknowledged that i can be billed. so when i got my bill, i was able to dispute it and got the charge removed because i quoted from the member handbook including detailed information on exclusion and inclusion and kp acknowledged it was an error. so takeaways from my experience are:

1. know your member's rights. you have the rights to the latest copy of your member handbook/member benefits. make sure you ask for it with information on all the inclusion and exclusions. it's alot of pages but read it so you can be informed of what's covered. ask for a translation in your language if you prefer (it's part of your rights).

2. if you question the cost of something and you're a kp member, ask them to bill you so you can dispute it.

3. if kaiser charges you for something that is a covered benefit, it's considered fraud. file an grievance and/or appeal with them first. if it doesn't get resolve or address within 30 days, you should notify dhcs (for medi-cal), cms (for medicare), and/or dmhc in general so an investigation can be opened. let these organizations know as well if you see quality related issues. if they get fined, they lose fundings and accreditation.

be your own advocate and know what are your rights as a patient!
