2 stars only because the awesome, underpaid staff is so stellar.  i want this hospital to be great....really i do.  have never stayed at sg but have had er visits for stitches for self and child. 

recently, i had a scary incident at home and called 911.  the wonderful paramedics were able to address it at home but were very forceful about my going to hosp to get checked out.  i told one of them i wanted to go to to suburban because that's my doc's hospital, but since i live so close to sg, they said that would be impossible.  i was told in the past by a much more assertive woman i know that if you push it, they will comply.  but i didn't.

the er nurses were incredible - angels. the docs were very nice and seemed knowledgeable.  they could have let me go home, but decided that i should stay overnight to be on the safe side.  i refused some meds-a shot to the gut. whaaaaaaaat?  no.  it was about 2 am at the time.  i could have walked out, but my husband and the docs, i decided, were right.  that's when things went downhill. 

the room i was assigned to was right next to nursing station.  so very noisy.  it was literally freezing in there.  not enough blankets to be comfortable.  the nurses were lovely but they kept coming in and out instead of doing what they intended to do the first time.  then they'd burst in, throw on that damned stark white overhead light and ask 25 questions that required cogent responses.  problem with this and probably most all hospitals is that cya and $ hold precedence over patients' health.  this is the *hospital policy*, not the employees' faults, but they lose good people because of it.  

finally a doc came in, said he would have let me go last night and kind of muttered about the fact that 2 short procedures would/could be done before i left.  but no one came to do them.  i waited for hours.  finally i found my nurse and said, "i'm leaving and will take responsibility for not having the procedures.  made an appt w/my doc and he'd take care of it. true, i did make the appt and he said he could do one of the procedures. he felt the other was not necessary.  

she summoned the the way overworked "hospitalist," who said i couldn't leave w/out the procedures.  she didn't mention the magic exit, which is to sign a release stating i didn't comply w/medical directives or whatever.  i said i "need to get out of here."  patients were ill all around me, coughing like they had the worst pneumonias, whooping coughs, etc.  i thought hospitals were very concerned with people catching infections while there and wanted them outta there asap, also $$$. i was going crazy.  finally had the 2 procedures.  then the waiting till i was told of the results and hopefully, released.  i tried to find my nurse, over and over and over.  finally found her and she said i'd have to sign the release. i said, "hey that's fine but *i* complied, i did the 2 tests. you guys haven't held up your side of the bargain...i should have had the results hours ago!"

she said the hospitalist had to sign the release! omg. she finally got ahold of her.  the woman looked like someone had dragged her behind their car.  she's young, very smart and competent, but they are killing her! i actually felt sorry for her, everyone was calling, approaching her, pulling at her.  that is *just* inhumane.  these cheap arse hospitals lining ceo's pockets with money and understaffing to keep it that way should be thrown in jail.....for life.  she was very nice, pulled up my results, signed my forms and i was so outta there!!!!!!  i could have cried, i was so frustrated and needed to get out of that place. 

this was disorganization at its worst.  the nurses were, overall, incredible.  but no matter how good you are, you can't do this job alone or be pressed this hard and retain your quality and/or your attitude!  i totally get that. 

at the *very* most, in the am, i should have had the two tests (15 min at most), gotten my results immediately and been sent on my way.  if they had needed the bed, magically, i prob wouldn't have *needed* the tests anymore. 

this place needs to get their act together and treat their employees right.  hire more people and get your procedures in place.  i realize there are  priorities among patient care, but a hospital or any health care facility, had to have have enough committed, serious people so that you can keep the process moving efficiently.

my doctor at kaiser vallejo is awesome. i've seen her for 15 years. she referred me to bariatrics back in 2005 because i was very challenged losing weight and was at 320 pounds. i went to the kaiser bariatric program in richmond ca, and yes, they make the patient go through all kinds of psychological tests and all kinds of classes so we can make an informed decision about whether or not to have weight-loss surgery. here's my warning for anyone thinking about having radical weight loss surgery. they'll teach you about not being able to take nsaids, drink alcohol, eat more than 5g of sugar, no time-release or extended-release medications, etc. the problem: you don't know what is yet to come. i developed osteoarthritis years later. what is the treatment for osteoarthritis? nsaids. unless you have ever had osteoarthritis, you don't have any clue how painful your life is going to be. the only pain-relieving alternative (legal and permitted by kaiser) is narcotic. percocet works really well on osteoarthritis pain. but it wears off after 3.5-4 hours. that means on really bad days you take 6 of them. a 30-day supply is 180 pills. 

kaiser used to provide 200, so there was always extra and refills were about every 4.5-5 weeks. then the government's war on opioids kicked in, and that overshadows patient needs. if someone is in pain, and has no other options for pain control, too bad so sad. sucks to be you. now kaiser limits to 90 tablets for 30 days. they wear off after 3 1/2 hours so that means more than half of the day is spent in pain. and there is no other option. i've complained all the way up the chain at kaiser to no avail. there is not another option and no fix. my recommendation to anyone considering bariatric surgery is fine out before you proceed what your options are if, 15-20 years down the road you've got arthritis that has you in pain most of the time.

all of that said this kaiser is awesome. i just wish they recognize that some patients are in real pain and are falling through the cracks and they need to find a way to address it.

i am an rn with a master's degree and was also an aprn for 10 years. having been a healthcare provider for many years, i am saddened to write a negative review of a hospital.

i was sent to the er by my primary doctor's office. when i arrived at ascension seton hays county er in kyle, the waiting room was not overly crowded, and it was evident some of the people were not patients but family members of patients. i was optimistic for a quick visit. 

i made sure to confirm that not only the hospital but all related to my care would be in-network with my medical insurance. i knew seton was in-network, but i did not want anyone involved in my care who was not in-network. i know seton has not been very good about this in the past.

after i was triaged, i was told to sit again in the waiting room. since i had to use the bathroom, i was directed to collect a sample. sitting in the waiting room holding a container of urine on my lap felt incredibly awkward. in fact, i was so embarrassed that for part of the time, i felt compelled to put it in my handbag. 

when i was called to the back, i was led to a stretcher in the hallway. that is where i remained throughout my care from assessment through treatment through discharge. 

way back in nursing school, i was taught to always introduce myself by name and role to each patient, for instance, "hi. i'm sandra, and i will be your nurse today." i consistently did this throughout my career regardless if i was wearing a name tag or id, and i strongly believe that every provider in healthcare should do the same, from technicians to nurses to physicians. during my visit at seton's er, some staff did introduce themselves to me such as ashley (the triage nurse) and the er doctor. however, there were others involved with my care who did not. 

from my place in the hallway, i had a front row seat to everything. the patient in the room next to my stretcher was obviously dying. family members sat next to and stood near my stretcher. i felt like i was intruding on their grief. as a caring person, i wanted to reach out and provide support, but i kept quiet since i really should not have even been aware of what was going on with them and the patient.

at another point, i heard a commotion going on behind the head of my stretcher. it was not particularly loud, but i heard security involved, and i felt frightened. i did not dare turn around to see what was going on, but i did watch as security walked a man in handcuffs down the hallway. i hope i had not been in any danger.

when my iv was removed, a band-aid was placed in my antecubital space where the iv had been located. shortly after, i noticed my arm felt wet and cold. i looked down and saw that i was bleeding profusely and that my beloved sweater was getting soaked with bright red. a nurse (well, i assume she was a nurse; she never introduced herself) brought over a bottle of hydrogen peroxide and a stack of gauze to remove the blood. she started the process pouring the peroxide on my sweater, but it would take a while to remove such a quantity of blood, so she left me with the supplies to continue working on it myself. finally, i got my sweater mostly clean, but i was left very wet and cold.

it was taking a long time to get final lab results, and then i learned that the lab had lost my specimen! how does that even happen? is the lab not in the same building? a mishap like that does not instill confidence. hopefully the lab does not also accidentally mix up samples or misread them or misreport them.

i spent almost 4 hours at ascension hays seton to have a few simple tests done (no imaging) and a medication administered (a push, not a slow drip). it was not like the er was chaotic. in fact, i watched many staff sitting behind the desk for much of my time there.

close to the time of my discharge, i was approached to sign a consent to treatment. it seemed quite late to be asking for that. i was feeling so frustrated by that point that i signed the various forms without reading anything. i was also told that with insurance i owed $*** just for walking into the er (the amount did not include tests, etc.). she wanted to collect money right there on the spot. i handed over my credit card, thinking this trip to was the biggest waste of money and time i could have imagined. i dread thinking about the remainder of my bill still yet to come.

every staff member i encountered was nice, and i appreciate them. still, i would not recommend ascension seton hays er in kyle. obviously, i strive and wish for good health and hope i never have to go to an emergency room again. however, if i do, i will first check into my other options before heading to seton.

if the apple store and chick-fil-a had a baby who said "i want to be a hospital when i grow up," this would be that baby's dream fulfilled.

"i'm so sorry you're not feeling well."
"i sincerely hope you feel better." 

i was laying on the bed outside the ct machine room when a random nurse passed by and asked me if i was cold and if i wanted him to bring me a warm blanket. i already had a blanket, but he brought me a piping hot one and folded it over me like my life depended on it. the only thing missing was "have a blessed day" and some waffle fries. 

everything was fast too. the last dc emergency room i visited left a lot to be desired...like medical care. after three hours of waiting for a bed and six hours of waiting for an ekg, i was asked to leave at 2 in the morning and come back the next day, so they could "free up some beds."

i had outpatient surgery here this week. what a rollercoaster 

i had to arrive at 530a for a 730a procedure. i haven't had surgery since i was a child, but that seemed fine. until we got there and they didn't start calling patients back until almost 545a! seemed a little unprofessional. 

the nurses and techs who helped prep me were fantastic. super sweet and talkative which really helped quell my nerves. the anesthesiologist also came in and he was fun to talk to. (i'd had a pre-op call with an anesthesia nurse the friday prior, which was also good.) different techs came in to do different prep tasks, then my surgeon came in just to chat through things one more time. he seemed to be in a bit of a rush which wasn't the case at my consultation, but it put me a little on edge again.

as soon as he left, it was like the green berets of rns came in and things were in motion extremely quickly. there was also a high school student from gpnhs in there?? they must have given me the happy juice before she came in because in retrospect that's freaking weird. anyway, very little chatting and then i was on my way to the or. 

there were tons of people in there which i assume is normal. but that hs student was in there too! (oh, what gpf money can buy!) i barely remember anything past moving to the operating table. it would have been nice for my surgeon to stop in again before i was asleep.

when i woke up in recovery all i could hear was a nurse telling me to breathe deeply, and telling me that my surgeon couldn't find my husband. nice wake-up call but whatever. i couldn't breathe well because i was in a lot of pain. her only response was "that's normal, you just had major surgery". whuh?? i get that i had to get the anesthesia out but the total disregard for my pain and comfort was really frustrating. it's also so bright in there. i had to ask for a towel to put over my eyes. that nurse and another were concerned about my oxygen levels at one point, but i literally couldn't breathe deeply. i was really sad that they couldn't give me any tips/tricks for taking better breaths, but just kept snapping at me.

i then went to my private recovery room. my husband came back (he was at home, which is just around the corner). from this point on i was still in a lot of pain and kept telling the nurse there. her only solution was to "go get the doctor so he could admit for pain management". giant eye roll. maybe you could just be patient and give me an hour to 1. wake up and 2. let the meds kick in? so rude. surgeon came in again to follow up on one issue that came up, but he was in a huge rush again. not that i needed him to stay by my bedside but it was literally like "went well. put ice on the incision. bye." 

the initial recovery room nurse went on break evidently, so then a nurse named nan (pretty sure. i was a little high still, lol) came in. she was great. finally someone who helped me breathe normally, and recommended that i sit up in a chair to help with both the breathing and the pain. nan was so wonderful. she took my vitals one more time.

then i decided just to get my butt home so i didn't have to deal with the rush there anymore. the initial recovery nurse came back and once my husband helped me
get dressed, she was stripping the bed before i even got all the way into the wheelchair. nice exit. see ya.

like i said, a rollercoaster. like anyplace i'm sure there are good and bad employees. at times this really felt like a factory, though, which was disheartening. i'm thankful all the people who took care of me did so, though, and i trust the doctors here immensely. the experience just leaves some desires.

been a cardiac patient for 20 years & moved to delray recently.
this week, i had the worst angina attack i have ever had. after my nitro tabs, no more chest pain, but i didn't feel right & my wife took me to this er.

day 1  emergency room
the main er dr. i saw, was dressed like she was attending a tennis match & was chewing gum with an open mouth, very unprofessional. her assistants were very professional.
i had not eaten all day & asked for a sandwich after being there about 5 hours. i was told 1 would be coming, but we waited. we all were joking that i was going to order a pizza.
an armed guard then wheeled in a wheelchair loaded with pizzas. i asked if he brought enough for everybody & was basically told stfu. very unprofessional. 
i saw an intern & she said i could eat. the nurses said no i can't. a male nurse (half my size) took a step towards me & raised his fist, like he was going to punch me. the 2 lead nurses made him back down, luckily for him. he was aggressive towards other er patients as well.
i was admitted for "chest pains" that i did not have.

day 2 cardiac telemetry unit
after being admitted to the cardiac telemetry area, the nurses were all amazing, each & every one of them. they care about their patients.
however, they were the only highlight of this journey.
an echo was ordered. they said they wanted to do a cta later in that day. as the echo started, i was told the cta would immediately follow. my wife was waiting in my room for a 20 minute test. after the echo was completed, (tech was great), i waited 20 minutes for a transport that never arrived. the echo tech wheeled me to the ct room for the cta.
i was prepped & put on the table, waiting 20 minutes for a nurse qualified to inject the contrast required for the test. none showed, but an emergency was brought in & i was removed from the room & waited in the hallway for another 30 minutes. i was then returned to my room. a little while later, i was brought back to the ct room & had the test. because of the delays, no results would be available until morning.

day 3 
after finally getting the results, the dr stated "the imaging indicated a 53% blockage, but we say it is 70%, so you need to go to the cath lab."
a cath was scheduled. the transporters came  & told me to remove everything except the gown. 
when i came out of the bathroom, they were both gone, as was my wife. wtf?
my wife returned in a minute, telling me they were called away for an "emergency in room xyz". my wife followed them to the nurses station, where they were just chatting. she also looked into room xyz & there were no medical people in the room.
it seemed the dr performing the procedure had not arrived yet.

their delays are causing me to spend more nights here. i am getting angry & have still not eaten today.

i demanded to see the head nurse. she showed up an hour later, with an attitude of "this is a hospital, we do what we want, how we want & when we want".
during this lovely heated discussion, the transport arrives & said something to the extent of "if you are not ready in 2 minutes, it will need to be rescheduled", raising my bp even more. my response was heard throughout the wing, "you need to learn some bedside manners, dude". 
he then transported me to the lab & he understood my frustrations after he heard about the numerous delays. we got along fine after that.
the test finished, people were really nice throughout.
because of the delays, i needed to spend yet another night.

mind you, the most nights i ever spent in a hospital for any of my heart attacks was 2 nights. now, with angina, i am spending 3 nights. huh????

day 4 cardiac step down
9am, they tell me i will be leaving today, just waiting for cardiologist & admitting doctors. the cardiologist's intern (really nice) came in before 11 and gave me a 1 minute rundown, not enough time for me to process what he was saying.
now, just waiting for the resident, who was another doctor that looked like she was out shopping, not attending patients in a hospital.
at 3pm, we were still waiting. i still have an iv connection in my arm & a heart monitor on. her intern finally shows up (much nicer than she is) & tells me i am being released. he also said that i can remove the heart monitor. i removed the monitor & got dressed. where are my new, expensive sandals? they were in my bag when i left the telemetry unit. not any more.
the nurse comes in & asks why i removed the monitor & i told her. she scolded me, but i understood why. again, the floor nurses were all great. the nurse removed my iv connection & off i went.

this hospital's great nurses are handcuffed by administration's greed.
the 2nd star is for the nurses.

it seems this hospital intentionally delays tests, to force patients to spend more nights. 
btw.... i have had angina throughout my cardiac history. i was never hospitalized for it
this hospital experience proves again, that...
healthcare in the usa, is not about health or care, only profit.

when we arrived at tham er, i immediately told the front desk my mom's symptoms and how we were told by her doctor to come here, in less than a min after filling out the 1, possibly 2 page document, they took my mom in right away, started running several different tests on her. she was seen by a doctor, x-ray technician, a nurse, all within 20mins.

is zero stars even an option? i would first like to say that if you are coming here for an elective surgery, joint replacement or others, do not come here, run as far as you can. 

my grandmother was scheduled 12/18/19 @7am for a total knee replacement, preop, or & pacu were awesome.

once she was admitted to the ortho floor (3rd floor) we were welcomed by the nursing manager, daniel bernstein, my grandmother is rolled into the corner of the hallway where we wait hours for her to get into a clean room. the hallway was "equipped" with a call light (silver desk bell), a pulseox monitor that was not being monitored at the nurses station because she is in the hallway, a privacy curtain that did not cover or provide any privacy and the list goes on (all pictured below). this not just a privacy concern but a real safety concern. the cords from the bed and all the machines she was hooked up too were crisscrossing along the floor where my handicapped grandfather almost fell! i asked for my concerns to be escalated when daniel said "we escalate this all the time", just blowing me off, noooo daniel i want to speak to someone else regarding this issue, so here i am writing this review as i wait. 

according to the academy of medsurg nursing: the practice of admitting patients to hallway beds while they await appropriate room assignments is patently unsafe and should never be used.

patients must be provided adequate space, privacy, comfort, and safety at all times. hallway beds do not provide clinicians with bedside access to equipment, such as oxygen, suction, and call lights, needed for safe provision of care. patients are at greater risk for falls and other adverse events if they cannot access a call light or be monitored appropriately by nurses.

she wanted the lights to be off, the thermostat adjusted, non of which can be done because this is a hallway. it was no surprise that my grandmother would be admitted to the hospital following her surgery so why was the hospital so poorly prepared? they have signs plastered every where saying "a quiet environment is a healing environment", well when you are in a hallway you can't just close the door. you are exposed to the chaos of the unit, the chemicals from house keeping, the constant call lights & phones ringing.

my last concern is for the nursing staff. how do you expect your nurses to provide adequate care if they can't even get to the patients bed. "your safety and health is our main concern", well then get patients out of the hallways then, safety is not a concern, money is. value money over patient safety, satisfaction & health.

you need to really ask how this is safe, how can you provide care to a patient in the hall, what if an emergency occurs then what? how about fire code violation? hipaa? i'm sure joint commission would love this....

this is long but bare with me. this place stereotypes people with mental health history. this is strictly for their er doctors and er intake nurses (some). i have past heart problems which were corrected in high school. i was feeling close to the same way the first time i had my heart episode and went to the er in mid november. i went in for heart palpitations, shortness of breath, extreme lethargic about to pass out feeling, and weakness. when i was taken to the er by my boyfriend, because who wants to call an ambulance on their lunch break in their work parking garage and drawl that kind of attention to themselves, when i got there, the intake nurses literally did not fucking care i existed as a human. it took the nurses or security guards who help wheel people in and out to tell them to open the door and let me in. the er intake nurse didn't give rats a$$ that i couldn't breath well, didn't pay attention to my boyfriend who was literally handing her an emergency card i keep in my wallet of all my allergies and medical history. my boyfriend told them my symptoms, they didn't even think about hooking me up to a ekg until i was in the er exam room, which if i can remember correctly was about 15 to 20 minutes after i arrived. the nurses were ok that day and the nurse who put my iv in kept moving it because she couldn't get the blood out...ok we'll go somewhere else?! so much pain while feeling like i could pass out. 

next the doctor comes in. talks about my symptoms, some history, so on. the moment i mentioned i was on an anti depressant with past history of anxiety, it switched his questions. it went from asking about how i was feeling physically to asking me if i was stressed, or sad, or anxious...so on with the other related questions. look, doc, i know the difference between heart problems and an anxiety attack, this is not an anxiety attack. so instead of ordering more tests he gives me an anti anxiety med, and let's me chill out for an hour or so. of course a anxiety med like xanax is going to chill me out and slow down my heart and breathing. been on them before in high school and anyone who has a friend in their residency at a top tier hospital can tell you, "yea that med is going to make your heart slow down and relax any symptoms." never once consulted a on staff cardiologist or offering to wait to have one come down because of my past history. given my previous heart problem, if anyone remotely understands the heart knows that things can come back and not in the same way as before!!! after this i was discharged and told if i have any more symptoms to come back. 

the next day and a half i slept, no joke, 18 hours out of a 24 hour day. i could still feel heart beats skip, still had shortness of breath just doing small things like going up stairs or even getting up to go to the bathroom. i didn't want to eat or even talk. so after a day and a half of not feeling like a functioning person, i went back.

this time the intake nurses took me seriously, hooked me up to ekg right away, and got an iv in me right away. this doctor took me seriously and ordered a ct with contrast to check for blood clots and did a few blood pressure tests based on laying and standing. everything came back normal. the moment i knew she looked at the most recent visit, started the, "are you sure you're not anxious," questions came out. in my head i'm thinking, "are you flipping kidding me?! does no one take me seriously?!" the one thing i will never forget the doctor saying to me is, " if you are feeling bad and don't get answers the first time, you shouldn't come back to the er. go see the doctors we referred you to the first time." i'm sorry what!????! i was literally doing what the discharge papers said. it's not my problem ( well kinda is if i die from not well examined heart issue) if you didn't exhaust all your resources to help or passed me along because you gave up. i started to cry. the only person who gave me hope was the nurse. she literally ask me, "do you feel safe to go home?" i flat out started crying, and said no. and told her i would never return here for any emergency. i told her i rather drive to a further hospital and die on the way, than come to this hospital again. she took that seriously and comforted me. i was discharged sent home waiting to see a cardiologist 2 weeks later. 

that cardiologist was pissed no one consulted a cardiologist on staff. i got an eco, heart monitor for a week, and a stress test, i have a problem with my sinus node and will need to have surgery. something that could have been solved and found in that moment if someone didn't profile me as a depressed anxious person!!! 

seriously, tell your doctors to stop stereotyping people with mental health problems. stop thinking that someone with a valid history of cardiac problems and a mental health past is just making it up and is just "anxious."

tl;dr:  mt sinai's er doctors refused to provide me with care for excruciating pain and as a result i nearly lost my life to sepsis. months after this experience, i finally have the presence of mind to post this review as a warning to others.

i visited this er at the urging of my doctor, who is affiliated with mt sinai. he feared that i might have an infection in my spine and wanted me to have some imaging and blood tests done because they didn't feel it could wait until the next week. my partner drove me to the er and we were seen very quickly - it was very quiet and we could only see 3 or 4 patients with relatively mild issues. we met with a resident, erik sherman, who did not listen to my situation at all, saying flatly that there wasn't much they could do for back pain. we asked again for an mri and the resident said "well, mris are very expensive and you might be waiting for hours," and my partner replied that our insurance would absolutely cover it and that we were fine with waiting as long as needed. 

my partner asked to speak with the attending, bess storch, and we again explained the entire situation and serious concerns our doctor had that led him to us to the er. dr. storch repeated that they were unable to do imaging and that i should follow up next week because this was "an in-office case."when she left the room, my husband called my doctor's answering service, yelled for the attending to come back, and he handed her his phone and begged her to speak with him. my doctor confirmed everything we had told them, and asked for the same tests we had asked for. begrudgingly, the attending allowed me to have an x-ray only.

we waited for a few hours for the x-ray and by the time they wheeled me back (i couldn't walk) a nurse came and said they had already discharged me. we waited for another 2 + hours and then we were handed the imaging report, which showed that i had a compression fracture on one of the vertebrae in my upper back. they said it was common and not a concern so we just left, completely demoralized and just happy to be out of there after more than 8 hours. a few days later, i was taken to another er by ambulance and was diagnosed with sepsis caused by a severe infection and an abscess that was pushing against my spine so hard that it caused a fracture. i needed emergency surgery and i spent months recovering inpatient. if mt sinai's er doctors had just listened to us and run tests, we might have known about the abscess sooner and my life would not have been put in extreme jeopardy. i nearly died. you should all be ashamed to call yourselves doctors.

unfortunately, i was facing the floor and have no idea who she is, nor do i remember what she looks like. once they finally got some pain and antinausea meds in me, they brought me upstairs. 
that's when things got better. i had some great nurses who were very helpful and attentive. dr. faihrman was absolutely phenomenal!!! she took her time to explain everything in detail to me during my 3 day stay. she didn't make me feel like i was just an assembly line patient. milton was a very cool cat. holly was a very nice gal, as well. i can't remember the names of the rest of folks who took care of me on the 5th floor, but they rocked!!! i'm thankful they all went to work those days. 
the experience in the e.r. this last time really leaves a bad taste in my mouth. i'll be having the matter looked into further for discrimination. nobody should ever be treated that way in an emergency room. i don't do drugs, nor do i drink. i wasn't unruly. i was in severe pain.

the mayo clinic was nothing like promised or expected. they don't even meet their own advertising on the website.  i asked my personal physician to make a recommendation to solve some of the health issues i was having.  he suggested the mayo because they give you a "team" of doctors to go over you from head to toe.  since some of my friends had also suggested i go to the mayo i agreed and my doctor set up the appointment and forwarded my medical history to them.  the clinic is about three hours from my home so i anticipated spending at least one night in a hotel. i was somewhat surprised when the first doctor, a cardiologist, saw me but knew nothing of my history.  fortunately i did bring a disk and some printed copies however he seemed overwhelmed. from my verbal description he set up a number of tests and appointments with other doctors.  okay, maybe this will work.  but no, getting appointments for tests and other doctors, in some cases, took months.  to make a long story short, i spent 5 months driving back and forth, staying in hotels, paying for meals and gas to find out there was no "team" effort and very little follow up.  tests would be conducted and results did show up on the app very quickly but i really needed a doctor to "translate" the results into layman terms.  the only real follow up i received was not from a doctor but from a pa who seemed to think high blood pressure and rapid heartbeat were not a big deal.  what they didn't tell me were the more serious issues the tests discovered that i only found out about those after showing my personal physician the results.  in my opinion, the normal operating procedure at the mayo is 1) see a doctor, 2) have him schedule tests and other appointments and 3) wash your hands of that patient and go on to another.
one other issue to be concerned about, their billing department is totally inflexible.  some of the cost of tests ordered were rejected by medicare.  i found out the reason was simple, they just needed a reason for the tests, a simple matter of coding.  billing would not budge, i was told that i signed a form saying i would pay what medicare did not cover.  yes, i did, but i never expected they would not bill it correctly.  i contacted the doctor who ordered the tests and of course got his assistant who was also inflexible, that i had to work it out with medicare.  unfortunately that is not how it works.
don't expect to get any real results from this place but do expect to waste a lot of your time and money.  the doctors are uncaring and seemed rushed, more so to get rid of you than to solve any health issues. they should really be ashamed but i doubt it.

this is a review for their labor and delivery part of the hospital.

i'm currently writing this in the recovery room, having just delivered my second baby (first one with el camino, first was with ucsf in the city). i just wanted to use this moment to rave about my experience this time around compared to ucsf.

from triage to l&d to recovery, all the doctors and nurses here are by far the most experienced, kind, knowledgeable and kind people i have ever met. due to covid i never got a chance to do a hospital tour, so i had no idea what to expect when i checked in 2 nights ago after laboring for 24h at home.

at triage i was greeted by nurse melissa, who checked me and i hadn't progressed enough to be admitted. instead of just sending me home, she asked me to walk the hallway for 1h to see if it'll speed things up. and it did, i went from 3cm to 5cm during that hour and was admitted right after.

the rest of the nursing team were all super pleasant, knowledgeable and explained every little thing to me without me having to ask. there's a really positive energy and rapport between the nurses so it carries through the whole bedside manner. my iv drip at ucsf last time was a traumatic experience, they couldn't find my vein and blood kept spurting everywhere. this time at el camino, they had a nurse who specialized in iv insertion and she did it painlessly and perfectly in one to without any blood. 

i knew i wanted an epidural this time, and instead of dictating to me when i should get it, they told me to tell them whenever i wanted it. i decided to walk for another hour before asking for the epidural. now let's talk a bit about the epidural. i had dr. k (forget the full name) and he was so good. no pain, super calm, and the meds took effect almost immediately. with ucsf i was in so much pain and the injection didn't even work the first time, i had to wait 2h for the anesthesiologist to come back to up my dosage. this time, the dosage was perfect because i had no pain but eventually i could feel the pressure as i was nearing 10cm. i could move my legs and could feel the pressure of contractions so my pushing was super effective. i'm told this is the perfect dosage and that the doctor is really good.

now onto the pushing phase. at ucsf (since it's a teaching hospital) there were 10+ people in the room while i was pushing. some were helping while others were just spectating. this time, i had one nurse stay with me the whole time helping me push, and once it got to a certain point she called my ob and she came and took it to the finish line. hardly tore, got 2 stitches and no hemorrhages. i tore second degree and hemorrhaged pretty badly with my first.

once baby was here, they moved us to the mother & baby section. since the epidural wore off rather quickly i was able to pee way faster than with my first, and the nurses in recovery were all super nice and accommodating. i also had a fabulous lactation consultant help me with breastfeeding, who really gave me the most helpful pointers that i never got with my first. when i was at ucsf with my first, i had a lot of pain in latching and the lc there told me that nothing was wrong and a "little" pain is normal. basically made me feel like a wuss. turned out my firstborn had a tongue tie and lip tie but i didn't get that diagnosed til she was already 3mo. of course by then my breastfeeding journey was already a hot mess and did not go well at all. the lc at el camino (stacey was her name) took her time to teach me how to latch and basically said that proper breastfeeding should never hurt. after 30min of training i was able to find a good latch and now my baby is breastfeeding really well. night and day.

anyways, i just wanted to take the time to give credit to an incredible group of staff. it's seriously night and day to my experience at ucsf and i wouldn't have known unless i had something to compare against. 

thank you for such a pleasant birthing experience. i never knew i would ever use "pleasant" to describe labor and delivery.

insanely overpriced lab services. our family doctor used to work with quest, and is now associated with the el camino health network. this means they send lab tests through el camino hospital labs, and then bill separately. a few standard tests that should have cost under $200 were billed as over $4000, then reduced due to a negotiated in-network rate with blue cross to "only" a third. i went to my insurance website and looked up the prices for the exact same procedures. quest is not even the lowest cost provider, yet their cost would have been less than a tenth of the final bill from el camino. so their prices are marked up 30-fold.
even if you have maxed out your entire deductible your copay alone will be higher than going to a different lab service. if this is your first procedure of the year, rest assured lab services at el camino are going to put a significant dent into your deductible. 
how can you avoid this? ask your doctor which lab they are using for blood work. if he does not know, ask the nurse who would take your blood, where they will send the blood. if they are sending it to el camino, you can insist that you want to use an independent lab service. you can then go with referral/instructions from your doctor to quest or a similar lab service. it will save you on average over $100 per test.

it has taken me awhile to bring myself to write this. late in 2018 my mother was admitted to riverside community hospital for the purpose of a tavr heart valve replacement through riverside cardiology associates. the tavr was scheduled for very early morning but almost immediately things started going wrong. we were scheduled to arrive at 5:30 am but due to a delay never fully explained the tavr was delayed till around 11:00. although we had been told that the tavr could be done with minimal sedation, the anesthesiologist said it would be full sedation just before she was taken away, contrary to the wishes of the performing surgeon. after the tavr procedure was completed, my mother moved to icu for two days.  we were told that tavr recovery is 2-3 days and then the patient can go home. although she was showing signs of complications they went ahead and moved her out of icu on day 2. instead, she was transferred to a floor where patients dealing with drug abuse were recovering. in one example, a patient across from my mother's room was so out of control they had several nurses trying to restrain her and, as i recall, even had to have a security guard called in. it was like a nuthouse. does the riverside community hospital protocol for tavr or any other cardiac patient call for being placed for recovery in that kind of environment?  to their credit, the nurses at rch did what they could with what they had.

as i said earlier, the usual recovery for tavr is 2 to 3 days. in my mother's case, her stay was five weeks before she finally died. during that time, her condition continued to spiral completely out of control with multiple infections, blood transfusions, invasive tests and no answers. she was eventually placed in a private quiet room but by that time she was comatose.  i met with as many as 5 different doctors a day but no solutions were forthcoming. towards the end the doctor visits became fewer and fewer (i know because i was in her room day and night). in fact i did not find out the final cause(s) of death till i got ahold of the death certificate many days later. there was no post mortem briefing. in fact there was no subsequent contact from the hospital at all. none. i finally managed to contact one of the attending physicians at his office but he did not tell me anything i did not know already.

in retrospect, all i can say is if i had know that rch could overrule a surgeon's judgment in the operating room, if i had known that my mother would be moved out of intensive care before she was ready and that the post op environment would be so questionable, i would never have let my mother proceed with the tavr procedure.

this place does not want you to get better. they only want to make money, and it's obvious at every level of care.

it started when i was encouraged into going in to "learn about the programs" in a very normal setting, but then as i told them the full extent of my depression which included suicidal ideation (but not plans) i realized that they tricked me into involuntarily staying there and my life was about to get a *whole* lot worse.

but maybe it was fine because there was individual therapy there right? no. absolutely none. the only thing close to therapy is a group session where you check in and no matter how badly you need help the therapist just smiles and nods. they don't even put all the mental health patients together, i was one of the only ones in a mostly substance abuse program, so i had trouble relating to everyone else. you never get any real help, the whole place is just a giant waiting room for the psychiatrist who only sees you for a few minutes a day, barely cares about your situation, and prescribes everyone the same medication no matter what, but you have to beg constantly to let you leave.

i should also mention that if you're stuck there involuntarily or ever sign out they place you on a 72-hour hold (business days btw, for weekends you're out of luck), and they lie to you about what happens afterwards. they say it doesn't matter anyways because they'll file for probate at the end of the period and you'll probably be out before the court hearing anyways. that's completely wrong... i learned later that they rarely ever do this. so that's another waste of 5 days because they straight up lied to me.

they keep everyone way longer than they should and the only reason anyone gets "better" here is you practically have to pretend you get better or they'll never let you go. i was kept an extra 3 days after i met all my treatment goals just to try a new adhd medication. a completely non essential purpose. have i mentioned they don't value your time one bit?

now onto the outpatient partial hospitalization program, which i told them i would go to only so i wasn't stuck for another week. a complete waste of time and every minute was excruciatingly boring. the "therapists" only read off a paper the whole time of really basic information. any actual input from the patients was met with, you guessed it, a smile and nod and no actual therapy. my depression actually got worse during this time because i was forced into such an upsetting, non-helpful environment. oh yeah and they kept me several days longer than they said they would...

outpatient psychiatry: i really should've left the hospital altogether at this point, but here i still was, going in to see dr. rahman. as time went on it became painfully obvious he doesn't care about helping you improve. i would go in and talk about how my meds are doing nothing for me and all he'd do is slightly increase the dose. he won't ever refer treatments that actually do something different like ketamine, and i wouldn't dare mention any suicidal ideation in these appointments in case they try to trap me here again.

bottom line: run. very far away. go to the lindner center, or literally anywhere else. this is the worst mental health facility i've ever had the displeasure of dealing with, and i've dealt with a lot. they do not care about helping you one bit.

beaware and demand to see all lab results and question everything as er doctors like dr. reyes are not trustworthy!!!   as a 3rd generation "redlander" that was born at redlands community hospital and who has defended it many times when i have heard people say. "if you need more than a band-aid don't go there,"  i am saddened to write this review but feel it is important so that others are not victim to having to pay double co-payments when they should have never been released but they trusted what the doctor told them.  the only reason i give it 2 stars is because the nurses and staff at the er were kind and helpful.  i learned the hard way to challenge what a doctor tells you and never leave until you physically see your lab reports, as dr. reyes convinced my family and i that i should be fine and even though i still had many of the symptoms and pain that i came in with. but dr. reyes told me "as long as i was not vomiting i would be ok."  i should have never been discharged with lab levels 8 times the normal range (the doctor never told me the number - not sure even if she had the complete report when she released me).  it should have been quite obvious to an er physician that the lab results grossly indicated a severe, aggressive, and active infection when in reality my parents and i were not told anything besides, "you have some form of stomach issue and your labs seem a little wonky," by dr. sonia-maria reyes.  great medical vocab don't you think?   eight times the normal level  is anything besides a "little wonky" especially after telling her that my symptoms had gotten progressively worse over the previous 48 hour period and i was worried as i was leaving for college in less than12 days.  not being a doctor, and never being told just how "wonky" my lab results really were, i unfortunately trusted the doctor and followed the doctor's directive to go home not knowing any other option and not realizing i could object and that she was just "practicing" medicine.  if i had not been discharged and would have been admitted and started on iv antibiotics that day, i am certain that i would not have had to suffer another two days at home hoping that what the er doctor prescribed was going to eventually help, when in fact it did not and i was back at the er on 2 days later, to then be admitted and be charged yet again!  it was my primary doctor's office that called my mom to check on me on monday and was appalled that i was sent home with the lab results that they saw.  my primary called and talked to the head of the er and i was told to immediately return to rch to be admitted and stayed for 2  1/2 days on multiple iv doses of antibiotics.   i had no problem having to pay my $575 co-pay from when i was admitted but then i received another bill for my first er co-pay another $250 which would not have had to be paid if i was admitted the first day as i should have been.  
 i sent my bill and concern to rch's appeals process and never heard back so i resubmitted it.  i actually received a letter this time but it stated that i still have to pay it because "both my parents and i were made aware of discharge plan."  it would have never happened if i or my parents were made aware of my actual lab results so again i urge everyone to challenge everything the doctor tells you, have them show you proof and do your research before you let them kick you out - i now understand why medicare now institutes the "hospital readmission reduction program" that does not pay the hospital for discharges that had a readmission within 30 days.  maybe all insurance companies should look into that for all age patients to protect them too!  i hope rch will reconsider and reimburse me for the additional $250 that i should not have had to pay, but regardless, i will never just believe an er doctor again - i will sit in that bed until i physically see all of the results and take time to look things up as they are many reports online about similar lab results that i had and even some that were less than mine where patients were not discharged!  you have been warned - be your own advocate for sure!!!

my poor mother died at age 50 in room 336 at the csu department on 01/19/20, due to medical negligence from dr. rojas, dr. sucha kim and dr. seneviratne and other administrative workers such as lupe. 

my mother was diagnosed with end stage cancer, after experiencing pelvic pain in sept of 2019. doctors ran tests after tests and could not pin point the origin of the cancer. my mother received so much sedation, much more than chemotherapy, to the point where she couldn't myself or my family. dr. sene had his chemo nurse administer 3 rounds of chemo in november, discovering that it never helped her, in january 2020. we were never told as a family that her cancer was aggressive, the fact that it would cause fluid build up in her lung, leading her to life support. we were told last minute, that she was going to rehab for two week in november-december 2019, knowing that she was not okay, since she was already having all these health complications. we were never given an exact prognosis nor did receive a concrete answer as to what kind of cancer she had. long story short, my mom was unfortunately transferred from ucla ronald reagan, back to bad samaritan, at the end of december. dr. rojas decided that a vats surgery would help minimize the excess fluid in her lungs and that it would help her breathe better, otherwise she would drown. little did we expect, that the stupid vats made her a lot weaker, leading to be dependent on life support at the csu department. that it would not only mess up her lungs, but also cause heart palpitations to 150 beats per minute.

why was my mom sent to rehab with no chemotherapy or other cancer treatments? as an oncologist, he failed is as a family. why did rojas allow my mom to get this dumb surgery? as a pcp, he failed us. and where was dr. sucha kim to tell prevent all this from occurring. as a pulmonologist, she failed my mom, myself and my family. why did lupe treat us like shit, and not offer an therapeutic techniques when my mom needed it, when she had bad anxiety.

   i had a large tablet lodge in my throat at home when i tried to swallow it, and barely had an airway. it was like trying to breathe through a coffee swizzle stick.  i was losing oxygen, and seeing glimmering floaters in my vision and couldn't feel my fingertips. and was starting to pass out. luckily i am an rn myself and am very good at handling emergency situations, and through the grace of god, managed to keep a cool head. 

  i knew i didn't have time to wait for an ambulance, and after failed self heimlich attempts, signaled my friend with my hands to grab her car to drive me directly to the er. as i was reflexively trying to cough and breathe, the tablet shifted to a spot where it completely blocked my airway, and i fell to all fours and almost passed out in the driveway. luckily it shifted back to the "swizzle stick" position, but then just continued to alternate between swizzle stick and complete obstruction. 

  "fortunately " i made it to the er. my friend drove straight up to the front of the building and burst through the doors with me in tow, explaining that i was choking and didn't have an airway. 

   i was handed a clipboard, "please fill out this paperwork (asking for name, address, insurance info etc)."  i desperately wrote "cant breathe - pill" in jagged, panicked handwriting and pointed (as in "please let me go there") to the er patient area behind her.  "no, we can't help you until you fill out the paperwork."

  at this point an rn walked behind the desk, and i showed him my note, and pointed to the door that lead into the patient area with the most imploring look of my life, and he begrudgingly let me in. 

  he told me he was going to take me to a room and let me wait there.  afraid to be left alone and knowing i needed immediate attention or could die, i grabbed his upper arm. i didn't think it was too tight, just really really scared and urgent. he immediately spun on his heels and reprimanded me like a 4 yr old, "no no no! do not touch me like that, or i won't be able to help you. you are still breathing mam, you can wait until we're ready for you."

   shaken, the anger now starting to kick in now that i wasn't wholly absorbed with saving my own life, i walked straight back out of the double doors.  "i'm leaving now, it's out - thanks for nothing!!!!" as the nurses' station, full of qualified staff standing behind the counters doing god knows what, looked back at me with slightly confused but mainly empty, "just another day" stares. 

   i shudder at the number of people that must have died at this er's hands. i think of all the poor family members who have been told, "i'm sorry, we did all we could."  so i'm writing this yelp review to let you know - they didn't.  avoid this er at all costs.

doc_text:
this review is for the birthing center at sequoia hospital. like several other yelpers here, i too, had a wonderful experience delivering my baby at the birthing center a few weeks ago.

leading up to the birth, sequoia gave us all the information we needed. we attended a helpful orientation one month before the birth, and pre-registered ourselves so the hospital knew our due date and when to generally expect us. 

i began labor two days past due, and gave sequoia a call at 2am to let them know that i thought i was in labor. they were clear, calm, and provided instructions on coming to the hospital, where to park, etc. 

as soon as we got to the hospital, we were greeted and they had very short paperwork for me ready. after a few quick forms, they got me into a room and checked out a few things. once it was confirmed that i needed to stay, they got me settled into the room and we finished up the paperwork.

i'll spare readers my long birth story, but the major takeaways were-- sequoia has amazing nurses. literally, the best. i was at the hospital for a total of 96 hours and had several different nurses (they work in shifts of 12 hours each). each nurse was extremely well trained and highly competent in their respective area. i felt very well taken care of and appreciate that each nurse that clocked in took the time to read my birth plan and get familiar with my wishes. a special shout out to nurse ute who was my nurse during delivery. after a long and frustrating time laboring slowly, ute started her shift by instilling the confidence in me to have a baby that day. sure enough, my baby was delivered just as ute's shift was ending... and she stayed with me the whole time i was in labor.

sequoia also has fantastic doctors. my regular obgyn was out of the office during my delivery, but the other on-call doctors, dr. kassis (who delivered my baby and was super encouraging) and dr. rao, were absolutely fantastic. the anesthesiologist, dr. bradley, was also extremely skilled and delivered my epidural quickly and efficiently.

lastly, sequoia gave me everything i needed to take care of myself and my baby when i got home. as a first time mother, i had no idea what i needed to take care of myself. in the blur of labor, i didn't realize that sequoia had packed several bags of "after care" materials for me. it wasn't until i got home, i realized sequoia had given me everything i needed to heal at home.

thank you to all the nurses, doctors, cleaning staff, culinary staff, and others at sequoia for making this a memorable experience.

i had a negative experience at the er. i had never been to sequoia or used dignity health before, and *only* came here because it was the closest hospital near where i was. i came in with some of the most frightening symptoms of my entire life, that i had never experienced before, and that were horrifying. could not breathe. body was going numb. lightheaded and dizzy. felt like i was going to pass out. 

as soon as i got there, the doctor labeled me as an "anxiety" patient right away, upon my arrival, even before any tests were done. he even said things to me like "you are agitated and argumentative just like my other anxiety patients" all while i was frantic about not being able to breathe and was begging for help. i couldn't believe he called me those words; i was going through such an awful experience, he could have been more empathetic. the doctor seemed irritated that i was there, and discriminated against me using this label, as if having "anxiety" was my fault, that i could control what was happening to me, or as if these physical symptoms were not 100% real. 

so during my er visit they ran several blood tests and the doctor gave me ativan eventually. the ativan did help a little bit to calm me down, but my symptoms were still there (i had been having them for about a week). the doctor came in and was adamant that i had to see a psychiatrist. his tone in telling me this was condescending and rude. he made all of symptoms out to be a mental illness, and i 100% know that they are not. perhaps having these ongoing symptoms for an extended period of time resulted in anxiety, but this is not all due to anxiety. i was trying to explain my core symptoms to him - but he kept interrupting me. he treated me like i was not worthy of his time, like i was some sort of drug addict looking for pills (in this case just a human being looking for a diagnosis). 

the er doctor made it sound like i just hop around from er to er wasting everyone's time, even asking me "how many times have you been going to er's for your anxiety" and "when was the last time you went to the er for your anxiety" and trying to reprimand me and shame me for going to the er. well guess what, i don't regularly go to the er. i went one time recently, in the prior week, when all of this started, for similar symptoms. but that's it. and nobody at that time said anything about it being anxiety. they actually encouraged me to go back to the er if i didn't feel better...which is what i was doing! 

so bottom line i left the er after about an hour with the same underlying symptoms that i had and have been having for over a week now. it has been several days and i have the same symptoms 24/7 but they have gotten worse. i'm fatigued and out of breath. i can't even fold my laundry without taking naps every 10 minutes. i am very athletic and in shape but can barely walk without wheezing and gasping for air. 

i feel traumatized now that i was shamed for going to the er, and labeled and treated as an "anxiety patient". i know something is wrong with my body right now. i have a serious chronic health condition already, and i went through years of symptoms where doctors like this one labeled me as an anxiety patient. i was told that everything was anxiety. well, it wasn't. the doctor was quick to judge and overconfident in his diagnosis (after seeing me for such a short period of time). if its not a heart attack or a blood clot then...it's...anxiety? no, not in all cases.

the doctor that initially encouraged me to go to the er said to go to stanford. she never mentioned this hospital, even though it is closer to where i live. now i know why.

edit: i spoke with a psychiatrist who urged me to get medical attention. he said he could only prescribe me medication to calm me down as a result of my stress in having to deal with this, but my core symptoms are not due to anxiety. i am working with my doctor to figure out what this is. it could be gi related, heart related, or lung related. so, nope, not anxiety. it causes anxiety, but my severe ongoing shortness of breath from the last couple of weeks is due to something else. the er doctor at sequoia hospital refused to listen to or believe any of my symptoms. my doctor was pretty shocked when i told her what happened there.

i went to the sleep lab after a referral from my doctor at tripler. i have tricare prime and so far so good on the insurance front.

lady parking security guard was helpful and walked me over to the security check on. she had really nice hair. dude who took my temperature and gave me my name tag was friendly as well. i was very psyched up because my sticker read "destination: sleep."

ruth at the sleep clinic was very kind and gentle with me while dealing with all the electrodes & sensors necessary for my test. 

i would have preferred if the sleep rooms had full size beds instead of the tiny twin size they have now. i kept worrying about possibly falling out of the bed which i suppose is probable for folx with various parasomnias. 

the only reason this is not a 5 star rating is the parking situation. i got validated parking at an outpatient rate of $3 versus $24. coolio. however, when i went to leave, the parking workers don't take cards. only cash or check. who still carries checks with them? i mean, i have checks because i'm a somewhat responsible old millennial, but i don't carry them around with me so i can inconvenience people at the grocery store anymore. 

i was instructed there was an atm in the hospital lobby so i reversed my car and parked. keep in mind that it's about 5:45am, the patient lobby is closed until 7am. i can see the atm from outside the locked doors; it's blue lit lettering taunting me. i am sleepy and i just want to go home, but no say the parking goblins. i am now sitting in my car awaiting the lobby opening. 

on a brighter note, there is a charger for electric vehicles right as you enter the garage. it takes cards. $2 for 1 hour charging on top of your parking fees. 

also, the closest open coffee place is a 10-15 minute walk. normally that'd be no big deal, but as i said, i came here to sleep. i have electrode goop in my hair. i'm not wearing a real bra. i'm donning birkenstocks with socks ala my romanian father-in-law. i'm foggy and attempting not to sleep in my car so i'm not sure questing for coffee in an area of the city i've never been in is wise. i didn't bring my sword so i could go link on any chickens i find and if you can't destroy things with a sword what's the point of a quest???

update: lobby opened promptly at 7 am. atm fee is $3.95. so all in all it cost me $3 with validated parking, $2 to charge my car while waiting for the atm to be accessible, and then $3.95 to withdraw $20 to fulfill my debt to the parking goblins. total: $8.95 and an hour and a half of my life i can never reclaim.  finally pulled up to the parking kiosk and paid, got my change and said thank you. goblin just blinked while furrowing at me. i expect this sort of bedside manner from doctors, unfortunately, but man, the goblin could have been polite back. i weep in sleep deprived silence as i drive home after nearly being hit by an elderly lady while trying to go turn into the parking lot for starbucks. huzzah. 

tldr: a+ for ruth @ the sleep clinic. parking goblins are no joke and will only accept antiquated currencies- cash or check only to leave the parking garage. i do not have any rubies or kiddos so i'm not sure if the goblins will accept shiny gems or a first born child as alternate payment.

the negligence that is occurring at this facility that is "committed to providing you with the highest quality of treatment and support" is downright disgraceful!  they have no respect for patients or family wishes, and actively prevent families from being proactive with the care of loved ones.

our family's story as briefly as possible:  my 79 yr. old father fell at home and fractured his hip.  he was taken via ambulance to our small town local hospital.  of course, during these times of covid, none of his family were permitted to be with him.  he has quite a list comorbidities, so our small town hospital deemed his situation too critical to treat.    they recommended we transfer him to hmc for surgery, post surgery care and then on to a rehab facility.  to say we were relieved was an understatement but unfortunately, that feeling left quicker than it came.  our father was taken into surgery without notifying any of his 6 daughters, 2 of which are his medical poa's.  the first call one of the poa's received was that our father was out of surgery, he did fairly well, but his bp was critically low so he would spend the night in icu.  oh, and by the way, can you complete these consent forms with me!  yes, if you're following, this was after surgery, not before.  this was unsettling but fortunately, it wasn't "another type of notification call" and we just wanted to start the road to recovery.  well, i'll spare you all the emotional, in between details, but basically our dad laid in a hospital bed incoherent and non-responsive from thursday until the next tuesday when we had him transferred to another hospital!  i can't even describe the fear, frustration, and heartbreak my siblings and i endured during these 5 days.  we couldn't see him.  we couldn't talk to him.  to say we were living in hell is not an exaggeration! doc_text:
you can do better than this hospital. i delivered my baby here in jan 2020. he's my first child, so i don't have other experiences to compare this one to. while i generally had decent care, there were many things about inova alexandria that were not as advertised, and as a result, we struggled on a few fronts. 

first, they actively advertise that they provide nitrous oxide to laboring mothers. this was one of the reasons i chose this hospital. they do not. i was already well into labor by the time i was told that there was no nitrous available at the hospital. i had mentioned this several times prior, had discussed it with my physician/midwife practice (who exclusively delivers at inova alexandria), and it was in my birth plan-- no one thought to tell me that there was no nitrous until go time. 

second, once i decided to get an epidural (given that there was no nitrous and i'd been induced a long time prior), the anesthesiologist clearly messed up as he was setting it up. to the point where he apologized to my doula-- not to me or my husband mind you. thank god i didn't end up with something terrible happening on that front. 

third, since i was induced, i was in the hospital for longer than expected before delivery. they had the most uncomfortable bed known to man. i got no sleep, and both my husband and i went into the delivery completely exhausted as a result. birth plan basically went out the window. 

fourth, this hospital prides itself on breastfeeding support. it's everywhere on the walls, the literature, you name it. but guess what-- their support is lousy. i had to request help multiple times. it got to the point where i had to beg the head nurse to ask a lactation consultant to sit with me and make sure he was latching. breastfeeding is hard regardless- but at a "baby friendly" hospital where they tell you about their fabulous lactation support, and i did literally everything in my power to flag that there was a problem and i was struggling, they failed me. i saw at least four different lactation consultants. there was a lot of happy talk, but very little practical help. when it wasn't working, they couldn't help me, and i left the hospital basically hopeless. i had to hire a lactation consultant to come to my house the next day and by that point my baby was a big fan of formula. 

fifth- as it turns out, part of the reason breastfeeding didn't work for me was b/c i had severe postpartum preeclampsia that went undiagnosed while in recovery, even though we spent extra days at the hospital because my son had jaundice. my body was busy trying to keep me from stroking out rather than producing milk. thank god i was told by a midwife to make an appt within 48 hours of discharge to have my blood pressure checked. i might very well have died in my sleep otherwise. 

sixth, i had the worst experience with a nurse of my life there. one particular nurse insisted on drawing blood from my days old son in the most painful way possible while he screamed as i've never heard a baby scream before. she was ignorant, ill-trained, and thinking of her to this day makes me furious. other blood draws were a breeze compared to this because they were done properly and he never screamed again. she clearly had no idea what she was doing. 

seventh, my baby had jaundice and they did a terrible job of giving you any option but to have a giant, drafty, old school light machine wheeled into your room so that you- in a hospital with trained staff and having had no sleep in days- have to make sure that a tiny baby who cannot have a blanket doesn't take off the thin fabric that protects his eyesight, etc. it was awful. 

eighth, there is not really a nursery here. they make this clear on the tour, but you might want a hospital with a decent nursery. what they have is makeshift, drafty, and not appropriate for proper care. 

ninth, they literally never let you sleep. i'm not talking about the baby keeping you up. they come to check vitals constantly at all times of the day even when there's a do not disturb sign up. we went home having not slept in basically five nights, which led to a nightmare scenario for a brand new family of three. despite all of this checking, they still didn't catch that my body was shutting down. maybe that wasn't possible to do-- but it is notable that i kept alerting nurses to classic preeclampsia symptoms and i was repeatedly told that those were normal after having been pumped with fluids during labor.

tenth, i left never wanting to come back to this place ever again. it was a miserable experience despite the fact that there were some staff who were helpful and tried their best. unfortunately, i had to go back to their er two days later because they had all of my recent birth records and health history on file. here's where they actually saved my life, and i had a generally good experience with excellent staff- save for the lactation consultant who was horrible, insulting, and should be fired.

i recently reported monterey park hospital to the joint commission, the agency that accredits hospitals. i had many reasons, but here's a snapshot: 

 my mother was released from monterey park hospital on 5/24/2020. i just received the discharge summary today, june 2, 2020.
 a typical discharge summary is written with 24-48 hours of a patient's release because the information contained in it will be vital to the patient's aftercare. time, therefore, is of the essence.
 to obtain the ds (and address other concerns) for my 87-year-old mother, i had to write many emails--all unanswered--and in the final one, threaten to get "legal representation" to force the hospital to release a ds.
 my mother's attending physician explained the delay by stating that he had been on vacation. he also complained that he hadn't had a vacation in ten years, and that he and his wife had planned one for march/april, but those plans had fallen through.
 he further explained that when a doctor takes a vacation, he is allowed additional time to write a ds, which sounded to me like a bad excuse for turning your homework in late. 
 no provisions or safeguards are made for patients at monterey park hospital whose doctors go on vacation. my mother's attending physician insisted that the task of writing a ds could not be assigned to another doctor.
 the day after her discharge, my mother went to the emergency room due to pain from a leaking catheter. we had no idea why she had been catheterized in the first place. discharge papers from monterey park hospital did not explain the catheter, so emergency room workers were reluctant to remove it. a ds would have been helpful in that moment. a ds was also the first thing my mother's primary care doctor asked for when we took her in for follow-up care four days after her release from monterey park hospital. however, we had none to offer.
if the ds debacle were the only issue with monterey park hospital, i wouldn't be writing this review. however, there's more, which is why i contacted ericka smith, the coo, to alert her to the many wrong things that occurred during my mother's 5-day stay. but ericka smith was completely unresponsive. completely. she didn't even acknowledge that she had received my emails. she is either indifferent, incompetent, or reflexively anticipates lawsuits and stays silent as a matter of protecting herself.
leadership is reflected in the good and bad practices of any institution, so i don't think my mother's situation was an outlier, or the problem with monterey park hospital is due to individual "bad apples." i think the problems are systemic, and leadership is mute. this is why i alerted the joint commission. when lives are at stake--as my mother's was, and still is--a hospital can't be allowed to operate in this way.

i haven't been in a hospital since i was two years old having my tonsils out. seriously, several decades (like 6?). and during this covid-19 pandemic, a hospital is the last place i want to set foot in. but my doctor ordered an echocardiogram for me anyway and off i went to the imaging dept at legacy meridian park medical center. 

upon entering the main lobby, i was directed to sanitize my hands, secure my mask and had my temperature taken (96.8 thank you very much). the imaging technician, eric, came out and directed me to the procedure room. i had to put on one of those ridiculously small hospital gowns and lye on my side on the imaging table. if you've never had an echocardiogram, it's basically a test that uses ultrasound to show how your heart muscle and valves are working. the sound waves make moving pictures of your heart so your doctor can get a good look at its size and shape. it's totally painless, although the clear gel they use to get the instrument to glide over your skin is hella cold! being a big chicken, i kept my eyes shut tight and didn't look at the monitor as eric worked. my test took less than an hour and included an injection of dye to get a really clear picture. a technician from the physiology dept was on-call to insert the iv for the dye. he saw my anxiety and joked by asking me where i'd like him to stick the needle to start the iv. i told him i had no idea, wherever was easiest for him. "how about your neck?" he smiled and i laughed out loud. everything was ok after that.

my whole experience was phenomenal! every staff person i met was professional and empathetic. covid-19 protocols were being strictly followed and i couldn't have asked for better care.
