marian regional medical center had the best newborn baby and mommy care i could have ever imagined.  their doctors and nurses were knowledgeable, extremely attentive, and caring.  we were proud to have had both of our sons in this facility.  the experience could not have been better.

and then there is the emergency room.  our visits with our sick kids were anything but a pleasant experience.  they amounted to nothing more than:

"hey, your son has a fever and an ear infection, but sometimes fevers are a good thing, so just let it ride.  here's a bill for $500-700".  "he'll be able to sleep once he's exhausted from the pain."  we learned to rely on our physician for much better care solely.

today, i received a frantic call from my wife stating that her mom fell down the stairs, and she called the ambulance.  the ambulance brought her to marian.  when i got to marian, the nurses were dismissive.  i told them who i was and asked if my wife was with her mom.  her mother has dementia and can't always speak for herself.  i don't know what was done with my mother-in-law because the nurses wouldn't even entertain my questions.  the nurse there gave me a number to call but then told not to call because the nurses would be busy.  what the heck kind of response is that?  they wouldn't even tell me if she was breathing.

my wife provided them with legal and medical documents stating that fact.  the staff didn't review the documents my wife submitted adequately.  her mom's hospital paperwork contained nothing regarding a living will or legal responsibility.  the staff didn't give her the time of day.  additionally, due to covid-19 precautions, my wife still was not allowed to be by her side.  these actions appear to be contrary to the dignity health website.  

we called around the hospital directory and reached the floor manager who, unlike those greeting patients, was very understandable.  she put us through to the nurse treating my wife's mom.  the nurse exhibited professionalism on the phone and thankfully allowed us to speak with her mom.  her mom was very curt regarding how they handled her.  

the nurse ultimately notified us that they performed all necessary checks, and there were no fractures of any kind.  when we inquired about the possibility of a fracture she sustained in her spine, before this event, becoming worse as a result of the fall, suddenly, they spotted the fracture.  they would not pursue an mri to determine if the fracture became worse.  

in the end, they said, "good-to-go," gave her some pill and left her behind the doors to the emergency room lobby waiting for me to show up, alone, with her belongings inside of a trash bag.  my mother-in-law was so angry.  it's like they handled her akin to something in a production line.  

marian should not pretend to be filled with blindly compliant staff.  if it happened to any of their loved ones, you know they would be there as an advocate or as a visitor.  my wife wasn't a visitor wanting to spend time with mommy.  she was to speak for her legally and medically.  it would have saved time for everyone involved.  in this manner, people wouldn't have rushed to read the results of the examination and get it wrong.    

it's a tough job the er staff chose--no doubt about it.  however, it's human beings and their advocates you're handling.

in mid-march, just as the covid-19 virus was ramping up, my husband required emergency surgery, not related to covid, for which time was of the essence.  he had initially been taken to st. mary's where it was determined that they didn't have the resources to perform the necessary procedure and he would have to be moved to long beach memorial.  there was no guarantee that he would survive the short trip to receive the procedure. 

he did survive the trip under patrick's care and from the time he arrived at long beach memorial, my mr. received the best care that i could have hoped for.  from the surgical team to the ccu and icu nursing staff, from the nurse practitioners to the physician specialists, the care and professionalism were awesome.  it was apparent that each of the individuals caring for mr. had a personal investment in his recovery.  i was treated with great empathy, was included in the bedside change shift huddles so that i was informed as to what was going on, and any questions i had were answered fully.

because of the virus lock down, i was only able to stay with mr. for a couple of days of his two week stay before i was locked out but was encouraged to call the ccu and icu nursing stations from home for updates.  staff recognized how difficult the separation would be so they also encouraged me to bring his phone to the hospital so that, after mr. awoke, we would be able to communicate, making it a little bit less isolating for him.

i will say that there were a few hiccups at discharge time.  i chalked this up to the fact that mr.'s discharge took place just as non-essential employees were being furloughed and consequently a couple of non-medical things fell through the cracks.  i was pleasantly surprised (and relieved) when i received follow up phone calls from the nurse practitioners for several days following discharge.

i would not wish mr.'s medical situation on anyone but feel confident in saying that if it happens, the patient will be in the best of hands.

delivery room: why so many people to acknowledge?  my wife went through 4-days of labor induction that needed 24/7 care.  based on some recent blood tests, the doctors recommended we induce labor some 4-weeks ahead of the due date.  when there are conditions that can potentially harm the baby at full term, an ob may elect to use drugs, foley bulbs, and combinations to help dilate the cervix and trigger active labor.  they monitor fetal heart rate and mom's contractions continuously during this process.  the process is uncomfortable and sometimes painful, and can range from 2-hrs to 3 days, since every woman and pregnancy is different.  our efforts did not work out as expected, so we went for the c-section, regarded as a "nuclear option". the 4-day induction period was not a total waste, since baby still had time in the womb to grow and develop.

c-section: its sounds scary, but the planned c-section was fast (5-10 mins) and painless according to the wife.  the pain and recovery comes afterwards, since it is a major surgical procedure.  dr. adey did her magic to ensure a smooth delivery.  recovery is lots of rest and otc painkillers followed by light exercise and returning to a normal diet.

recovery: we got 3-days for recovery in the hospital, which gave me a bed to stay as well.  all meals for mom is free and delivered by room service, while for me it was $10/meal using vouchers.  it is during recovery where the baby rooms with us while mom recovers.  here, the baby will be poked, prodded, and tested to ensure good health prior to release.  as for the parents, you get a 2-3 day crash course in newborn care.  surprised we learned diaper changing, installing baby in car seat, burping, blanket swaddling, holding the baby, and feeding (finger feeding, breast feeding, breast-feeding with supplemental tube, and bottle formula feeding).  you'll learn how often and how much to feed.  for breastfeeding, they'll offer excellent lactation consultants and nurses who can also provide breast pumps.  don't worry if you have't picked out a pediatrician yet - the visiting staff pediatrician will help you administer tests, answer questions, and schedule postpartum tests until you choose a permanent one later.

overall:  highly recommend valleycare for labor and delivery.  free and fast wifi great to pass time during labor, and the nursing staff here is amazing.  pregnancy, labor, and delivery do not always go according to plan, so have faith and put your trust to the experts at valleycare.  thanks again to dr. adey for working her magic to deliver our son!

just fyi, when i recently looked to read more reviews on cascade behavioral health i notice they changed their website to cascadebh.com to escape all the horrible reviews on this website.  i think anyone that has had a bad experience should post it to their new website.  www.cascadebh.com
close to death!!! i almost died at this place
i am not a "baby that did not finish the program", as some of the 5 star reviews say.  in fact i have been in aa since 1986 and have worked the steps multiple times as well as sponsored people and all the other things we do to stay clean and sober.  i had to take opioids because i broke my femur, and i self admitted myself to cascade to detox, feeling it would be safer than trying to do it alone at home with my sponsor an aa friends.  boy was i wrong about that!  the worst 7 days of my life!!!
i would give this place no stars if it would allow it.
the day i got there they rushed me through the paperwork, strip searched me and stuck me in a freezing cold room with none of my belongings.
the nightmare began.
i lay in my bed for 7 days with absolutely no help or human contact other than the nurse that took my blood every day, and another nurse that gave me a couple of pills(which i thought were my antidepressants).
when my doctor ordered a copy of my medical records from cascade, ( 5 pages were missing),it showed  that they took me off all my medications including the anti depression medicine and so i could not eat, drink or sleep.
this will be hard to believe but they gave me a hallucinogenic drug.
i really thought i would die in there.  the only person i spoke with was my 2nd roommate for little short spurts while she was getting ready to get up and go sit at the table.  she was told not to talk to me.
there is an evil man that was the director of the facility (he used to be at milam in kirkland until he was fired)and the last night i was there he was upset because he realized i was there for only 7 day detox(all my insurance would pay for).  he threw an absolute fit throwing stuff around and then cut off all meds that night for me and my roommate.
that next morning an intern(doctor) came in( i could see his desk from my bed), after looking at my chart he yelled "how can you treat people this way?!!!  i am calling 911.  the director came, there was another doctor and they were all arguing about it.  no one called 911.  i could see he was alone at his desk for a moment so i summoned all the strength i could and used a walker to get to his desk and asked him "do you believe in your hippocratic oath"?  he said "yes".  i then said "please help me",

i had a stroke either while in treatment, or at the hospital and i had a psychotic break (most likely it was lsd mixed in with the pills they made me take before i left cascade), at uw they found an unknown substance in my blood, (lsd is not traceable).
please don't go here. there are doctors that can help you detox at home and can give you non-addictive drugs to help with the symptoms.
or go to a 12 step group like aa or na, there are people there that can help you too.  you are putting your life in the hands of insane, evil, money mongers that do not care about you.  please do get help if you are suffering from addiction, read the reviews about the place you are going.
i talked to a lawyer once i recovered from my stay, but he wouldn't take my case because he said because their were no lasting injuries i didn't really have a case. that was 5-6 years ago.

i delivered my daughter at this hospital on april 30th under the advise of my ob who said this hospital was great. i went in for a scheduled induction at 8am on the 30th and my first attending nurse was amazing. super supportive, nice, upbeat and reassuring. unfortunately i can't remember her name but i know she was from hawaii because we made small talk during the induction process. 

well i got to the point where my contractions were coming too rapidly and lengthy (coming every 30 secs for at least 45secs to 1 min each) for the only 4 cm i was dilated. so i elected to get an epidural being that the contractions were strong and i was dilating super slow; i went in already dilated to 3cm. fast forward and things started to move faster after the epidural and dialing the pitocin up quite a bit. the attending nurse was so sweet that she hung out slightly after her shift because she was determined to see my baby girl. unfortunately she couldn't hang out to that point since she was born at 9pm and her shift ended at 5pm i believe. 

fast forward again to postpartum. everything started out good.  but the reason i gave 1 star starts now. the room was freezing cold, i informed the nurse that it was super cold and the thermostat was not working. i was told that they would contact engineering and have them check it out. 2 hours later and freezing, nothing was done. i called again and finally a different person contacted someone who fixed it... temporarily.  of course after delivery things can be "less than tidy" and i consider myself a pretty clean person. well the cleaning crew did absolutely nothing but empty the trash in the bathroom. no one checked the bed/changed the linen, swept or mopped the floor or actually cleaned the bathroom. and unfortunately i had to be there for 2 days since my discharge time would have been too late in the night because of the required 24hour stay after delivery. 

the following day the lactation specialist, nicholette, came in to go over breast feeding with me. not once did she ask me about my personal situation e.g.) personal life and whether i have a partner to assist,  medical history, potential work schedule, nothing i think would be important to establish my personal feeding plan. i had a pacifier for my daughter because i couldn't stop her from crying. the first thing she did was tell me her name and write it on the board. the second was to take the pacifier out of my daughter's bed and throw it in the drawer and tell me "she doesn't need this, these are terrible" i was in disbelief and speechless. she never asked why i had it out but just shut down the use of it. she asked me to try to breast feed her so that she could see how things are going. i obliged and picked her up and attempted to latch. i explained to her that i was having some issues getting her to latch because of the shape of my nipple so i was going to try using a nipple shield that my doula suggested may help.  she asked if i tried different positions, which i had and told her.  i said i was going to try using a nipple shield to help with latching and again shut me down saying those are terrible and she will latch i just have to make her. keep in mind, i've just had a baby, i'm exhausted, i've been trying to breast feed, and my baby was crying quite a bit. now she's come in and told me that everything i've been doing is wrong. so finally my daughter latches, she asked me if she could help out. i said "sure." so she starts aggressively massaging my breast while my daughter is latched and i'm just sitting there because i can't get a word in because she's over talking me. a nurse comes in to ask me a question and suddenly she storms out of the room. she goes and tells the attending nurse, wendy, that i was "non compliant." wait... what?!?! she starts immediately asking me why i didn't want to work with her without asking me how i felt, if there was an issue, if i felt comfortable... none of that. just basically that i was wrong. luckily the pediatrician on call came in to take a look at my daughter and he asked about breast feeding and how it was going. i explained to him that she hadn't urinated and she was crying a lot. he suggested supplementing her with formula because she was likely hungry. well he was right! she sucked down 3 ounces of formula in no time which was what i was trying to explain to the nurse and lactation specialist.  

overall, the lack of room maintenance, communication, and bedside manner were definitely subpar. i definitely would not choose this hospital if i have another baby, and wouldn't suggest it to anyone either.

it's been awhile since i've written a review and since with the covid scare all the restaurants in town are closed i decided to try out one of our longest standing eateries, the powell valley health clinic.  since you can't just leave a single review at such a fine establishment, this is part 1 of 2.  starting off, i would say the curb appeal is better than in the past with multiple extra signs telling you exactly where to park which is helpful when you can't breathe, you're dizzy, and have no depth perception to begin with.  
   you're greeted at the door by what i assume is a welcoming smile behind that mask where you are asked additional questions to further accommodate you.  a hard dry cough, fever, and dizziness even gets you a shiny red sticker on your chest so that others know you've made reservations and you can use the disney-like 'fast pass' line.  a mask, some gloves, and bam! you're in!  
   the maîte d' is of course the first person you'll see, and as the position dictates in any fine establishment, they are very knowledgeable of past stays, have payment info and address on file, and will have any paperwork ready to go to speed up the process.  after just a few quick minutes of waiting...while staring at the assortment of magazines and wondering if i dared touch them...i was called in.  
   at this time i go back and they take measurements, height and weight, and then it's time to see my personal physician's physician's assistant.  some more vitals are taken here and then bam!  one step closer to salvation and feeling better!  next came the physician's assistant - finally! the person i was waiting for.  the physician is gone for the day, but the training everyone here has is impeccable..and if it's not, how would you know? 
     we went through the symptoms again and took a look at my tonsils.  then we called in a physician for a quick consult and take a swab of my tonsils and throat to grow a culture and wham bam, problem solved!  my problem?  i didn't wait long enough to see if it would go away!  silly me!  
     exiting was even easier than coming in with no lines or stops, and since they already knew where to send the bill for my visit i was back in my truck and headed home to try and not die!!  overall my stay left me feeling wanting.  i was in a lot of pain, hadn't been able to swallow since the night before, so no water or food but hopefully it would all work out.  i had no answers, only more questions, and pretty scared to be honest, but i have faith in the people put in place to protect me.  the staff was very pleasant in that small tight-knit country community vibe you've come to expect in powell, and so after saying very painful but socially required thank you's i was out.  
     i feel nothing but the best for this establishment and the people working hard to keep our community safe in these uncertain times.  they're at the front lines - not just when it's in the news, but all the time.  caring for you, your loved ones, and being there for all of us in our most vulnerable moments.  i came back to the powell valley hospital the next day, but as i am not yet done with my current stay i'll have to hold off on writing my next review - spoiler, this will include hotel and restaurant amenities!!

the birthing center at sutter davis is an amazingly unique and special place to deliver a baby. i'm so thankful to have heard about this practice. despite having to drive to davis, i have no regrets about picking this spot for my prenatal care and delivery.

for the vast majority of pregnancies (non high risk), their midwife practice will definitely do the trick. i made a point to meet most of the midwives, and i really liked each of them. i was comfortable with any of them delivering our baby. they were easy to talk to you, thorough, and assuaged any concerns i had along the way. they and the broader care team were also very responsive online and on-call.

ultimately, jenn taylor delivered our baby, and amusingly she was one of the few midwives i had not met during the regular prenatal appointments. however, she was awesome, and i'm so glad she was on duty when we went into labor. the vast majority of the staff we met in the birthing center during our stay, too, were really thorough and warm. 

the birthing center itself is really great. they are conscientious about evidence-based practices. they care about the details, like dimming the lights. you can also labor or birth in a birthing tub (though, note during this current covid19 pandemic, they temporarily do not allow the birthing tub for delivery, though you can labor in the tub).

i enthusiastically recommend checking out the obstetrics and midwives practice here.

what a roller coaster.

coming in, the temperature nurse was really sweet and brought me a chair to sit in while filling out the paperwork. they brought me in after a few mins to get my history, vitals and blood draw to check my troponin. 

trust, i've been in and out of the er frequently for sob, palpitations, chest pain and heaviness due to my history of cardiac arrest. 

triage nurse and ecg tech were very friendly. nurse told me they're probably going to monitor me to make sure everything's okay. 
i head back out to the hallway and finish the paperwork..

1.5 hours pass and i'm nodding off in the hard plastic chair. butt is numb and i feel cold. 
i ask the registration if they could inquire if i was going to be monitored like i was told (and what usually happens when i go to er).

the nurse comes out and says they're gonna do a 2nd blood draw after 2 hours. i ask about the monitoring, and she says they're just gonna take my ecg again with the 2nd blood draw... this was news to me. 
we vibed well but it didn't help with the miscommunication.. the reason i wasn't getting taken in was cause they were full, but just a little communication goes a long way.

after waiting 2 hours, i asked registration if i could just know what my initial vitals and labs were. 
every time i spoke with the older lady, she made me feel like i was such a bother, when all i wanted was some communication. she literally told me nothing other than they don't see that info and the charge nurse never got back to her (only after i stood near the registration window for 5 mins, sat back down and asked about my results the second time 15 mins later!)
this was what really discredited my experience at bhh. 
at my hospital, they require us to maintain communication with our patients regarding any delays and reason for delays so they stay in the loop instead of sitting out there wondering and getting frustrated; to acknowledge patients without attitude. 

man, this made me wish i just stayed home. 

after i was taken to draw labs for the second test, i asked the rn if they could just call me if anything was up. i was cold, tired, and very uncomfortable. 

the er doctor, who was very cutthroat and straight to the point (i dig that), came to meet me after i mentioned i wished to leave. he ended up seeing me twice and said "i'm happy to share good news..."  

i believe that i'm a very patient person. i understand that extended wait times happen. miscommunication happens as well, but complete lack of it and attitude was not something i came there for. i come in respectful and optimistic about the care and experience i will have, but that really turned me off. 

so, all in all, mixed feelings about bhh, but i would not come back. 

hopefully, they're nicer inside the hospital ‍

so here i am, a week after turning 20 sent here. i think, ok, i'll make the best of this to try and get better. boy, was i wrong. it's co-ed so they don't separate males and females. they also let psychotic patients roam free and terrorize the non-violent patients. i was there for a week total and i cannot even count on both hands the amount of times i was harassed, given death threats, unwanted romantic/sexual advances etc. men would sexually hears me and when i ignored them or gave them an answer they didn't like they threatened to kill me, shoot my family, etc. there was a minimum of 3 physical fights between patients a day with screaming, yelling, all of it. the more aggressive/violent patients would try to antagonize the others to fight with them for "fun" (for example one would repeatedly try to bait me into a fight by saying dumbass stupid bitch, fucking bitchass hoe white girl, etc after i turned down his offer of "wifing me up". there were a few patients like myself who weren't insane, just going through a hard time but were constantly scared and under stress of the aggressive patients.
i had a guy come up to me everyday telling me about conspiracy theories and his "secret pet monkey". the first night i spent and woke up my roommate was screaming at me in spanish calling me "el diablo" and poking me and trying to steal my belongings. staff moved me to be with a different roommate who was very kind and lovely. however with the constant fighting and screaming my anxiety was at an all time high. the dr at first refused to give me the medicine that works to calm my anxiety. they tried to also make me take ssris which had previously given me adverse side effects which i explained to them, yet they wouldn't budge. after my mom made a phone call to them and raised hell then they gave me the proper medicine for my anxiety. i was scared all the time in that place. most of the nurses treated u as if you were an animal at times. it was a very dehumanizing and terrifying experience.
i needed help at this point in my life, not to be further traumatized. the one good thing i can say about this place is they have good food. long story short though it's a free for all where violent and aggressive patients are allowed to go at you with little intervention, no protection from sexual harassment, and this is a sad reflection of our mental health system that a person like me ended up in the same place as some of these people. i demanded a 72 hour release paper and that's how i got out and am now going to my therapist and an actual helpful psychiatrist. also, there is no real therapy or therapists here. people just exploding and getting "booty juiced" (sedation vaccine administered through the buttcheek) all the time. i also will say the art therapists here who would lead programs where you would do art activities were lovely and wonderful people, and were some of the only actual staff who acknowledged the situation i was in and how i should not be there.

i've been coming to methodist for my obgyn needs for a few years now.  in, fact i delivered my son here!  this review is a bit bittersweet as my current health insurance carrier is terminating their relationship with methodist, so looks like i'm going to have to seek out a new practice and that makes me grumpy!

anyway, as with most doctor's offices - wait times can be rather atrocious so i would advise trying to take the earliest appointment in the morning or the first available after lunch.  they do tend to run further and further behind as the day progresses (this is common with most medical practices), so just bear that in mind and bring along a book or your ipad (there's free wifi).  i've been a patient of two doctors in the obstetrics and gynecology department and i've been pleased with the interactions and quality of care i received.  even the front desk staff, techs, and nurses have been understanding and patient, even when i've been disheveled and bewildered (as a first time pregnant lady can sometimes be).

i was especially pleased with my stay in the childbirth center.  it's a smaller labor and delivery area compared to some other hospitals in the medical center, which i feel facilitated a quieter and calmer stay, and it enabled the nurses and staff to provide more individualized attention to me and other patients.  granted, i only have this one experience to draw my opinion from, but the nurses were just so extraordinarily kind and helpful during my stay here.  almost two years later, my husband still brings up how lovely everyone was to us during our brief three day stay here.  i had a traumatic (but not life-threatening) postpartum complication that was rather unpleasant to deal with and the nurses really busted their butts to make me comfortable as possible and continuously tried to seek a resolution to my issue.

anyway, highly recommend methodist - especially for the obstetrics and gynecology department and the childbirth center.  hopefully i'll be able to return to the hospital in the future, should my insurance get their crap together.

prior to my surgery, i had to come in for pre-op labwork and registration, as well as be tested for covid-19 as part of their policy. all patients must do so regardless of whether they have symptoms or not. the nurse was very nice and gentle with me, explaining everything as she went, apologizing for any uncomfortableness i felt. she truly tried to make it as easy as possible for me. i got a phone call the next day with my results (negative of course) and was then explained currently policy for visitors and what i needed to do the night before surgery, as well as the morning of. 

surgery day, i arrived. i was called back quickly and got put into my gown and compression socks and put into a bed and nestled under a super neat inflatable warming blanket. all the staff was very friendly and kept checking on me while we waited my turn for surgery. the anesthesiologist (chris lambert) was super nice. he cracked jokes to keep me from being nervous, and said he would make sure i had zero nausea when i woke up, because i always do. he kept his word - not one bit of nausea when i woke up after surgery. good man, thank you! 
the surgery itself was done by my own chosen surgeon (dr. chris park) so i'll leave that part of the review on his page, but it's fantastic. 
after surgery, i woke up in my own room. i stayed overnight because dr. park said he prefers that after what i had done, because he knows my pain is controlled and he is able to pop in and check on me. it seemed like i good idea, and would've been, had it went according to plan. but it didn't. 
dr. park came in to check on me and tell me surgery went great. at that point, i was in no pain, which was good. he told me to go on and call the nurse to start my pain meds, and i'd get them every 4 hours. i set an alarm on my watch for every 4 hours (something i learned while fighting cancer) to make sure i wake up and take them on time to stay ahead of it. he said one the pain hits, it's 10x harder to get it back under control. i called my nurse for pain meds at 7:51pm. i called again at 8:30 because she never came. she finally showed up at 9:20 with my pills and an attitude. by then i was in tears from the pain. i refused to let my husband facetime me because he would see how bad i was doing and i knew it would stress him out. (hospital has a no visitor policy, so he had to drop me off at the door and leave, and then pick me up the next day when it was time to go home.) i took the pills and thanked her. i reset my alarms since that obviously messed up my schedule. 4 hours later, alarm goes off and i request my pain meds. nurse doesn't show up til nearly 2 hours later, again. i'm in tears, again. i ask her politely if my chart says every 4 hours or every 6 hours in case i was confused from anesthesia when i talked to dr. park, since she was bringing them every 6 hours. she said "chart says 4, but you're not my only patient, so you get them when you get them." that's how my night went. when dr. park arrived bright and early the next morning, he was surprised to see me in pain and asked what happened. i told him, and he left the room immediately. i heard words being exchanged, and he came back in and apologized profusely for the experience i had because that's not how it should've been. he said my entire reason for being there was so that wouldn't happen, and i could tell he was greatly upset by it all. needless to say, after that, things were different.  i had a different nurse until i was discharged. i was immediately given morphine to knock out the pain, then set back on my original schedule of percocet every 4 hours. once they saw it was working as it should be (as it should have been last night had it been given correctly) i was able to go home. 
my daytime nurse was a gem. super sweet, very attentive if i needed anything, but i try not to call unless it's necessary. the food was delicious. 
other than that one night time nurse, my entire experience here with everyone was wonderful. 

** i will not name the night nurse. i only know her first name and it's a common one, so i don't want to put negative light on innocent people with the same name. i found out later that she was reported for her behavior, so that's all i'll say about that.

i'm giving this place two stars because there are some good and bad. i had a serious suicide attempt and i had voluntarily committed myself to walden. i acknowledged that i needed help and i was open to it--in fact, i was looking forward to it. as the days went on i felt more and more demoralized for the following reasons: (1) i felt deliberately disrespected by the nurses, many of them are super unprofessional and would make nasty remarks while the patients are present. i've had culturally insensitive remarks thrown at me when my parents brought me, i've seen a patient break down because a nurse said the patient was obnoxious to another staff. i've dealt with another nurse pressuring me to take medication, rogue from the recommendations of the psychiatrist. (2) it felt more traumatic to be there. there was a lot of intermixing in regards to the severity of the patients mental illness. there were instances where i'd wake up to shrieking. i've seen a 16 year old patient being sedated in a violent manner. (3) another thing i really hated was during visiting hours a nurse pulled me aside for more intake stuff. i valued my visits because it was that one time i could actually reconnect to my world outside of walden. i'm not able to spend nearly as much time with my loved ones. i asked the nurse if it was possible to do it another time but she said she can only do it during that time (i highly doubt it). 
there are patients of all sorts of age range: from 16 to patients roughly in their late 50's to 60's. regardless of who you were outside of the hospital, your sense of dignity is ripped away. i felt infantilized and like i can't be trusted. i feel like recuperation from mental illness is being able to trust yourself again but it's harder to do that when i'm being gaslighted by certain staff. feeling self-sufficient is a luxury here. 
i felt more depressed the longer i remained there so i signed myself out because i felt that this place was jeopardizing any chance i had at recovering. there were good parts--any part that does not involve the nurses. i thought the psychiatrist was helpful. i felt comfortable opening up because for the first time i felt respected and sane. my psychiatrist was completely transparent and respectful of my boundaries. i also felt the mental health counselors to be very helpful because they listened and worked harder than the nurses. i felt safer crying and actually voicing my concerns and fears.
if there were some structure and transparency, if there was more effort to advocate for patients--this would have been a much better place.

this is for the physical therapy department only.  

i've had the unfortunate luck of having multiple joint replacements and other orthopedic surgeries (before becoming kaiser member) at a young age. the reasons why were never clear though many doctors have tried to figure it out.  the most common theory is that because i have hypermobility but was very active from a young age, this has deteriorated my muscle skeletal structure and started a domino effect. 

i had good physical therapy following my surgeries and the replaced joints are not a problem.  however, i continue to experience profound pain and discomfort on my right hip which is my one remaining major natural joint.  x-rays show no reason for this. i went to kaiser pt multiple times but found that the treatments actually worsened the pain.  when i eventually said this to the pt (actually a very nice guy) he basically threw up his hands.  

this issue has affected me greatly and i am in constant pain regardless of trying things like meditation, turmeric, foam rolling, etc. etc.  i've even had to resort to strong opioids left over from my surgeries even though i had weaned off long ago. i finally decided to bite the bullet and pay out of pocket for a place recommended by a neighbor.  i had immediate relief after the first session.  here's what they do that kaiser pt does not:

- you do the exercises with the therapist monitoring as opposed to going home with an exercise sheet. this allows you to report areas of pain or discomfort as you do the exercises and it also allows them to try other things while making note of your comments.

- hyper-mobile people have distinct needs, and therapy modes that work for most may well not work for them or have to be adjusted. i'm now working with someone who specialists in hypermobile patients.

- the new place truly deep dives into diagnosis.  muscle skeletal issues are complex and there are a diverse set of reasons why x may hurt.  you may have weak hips, but your issue may go beyond that and there may be a reason as to why your hips are perpetually weak.  kaiser pt is great for people who neatly fall into the bucket of widely known issues and common prescriptions, but for people who need a more individualized care it is a black hole. 

- i barely did any exercises in person with kaiser, so needless to say they did not help with any stretching whatsoever. in my case, though i'm double jointed there are a couple of tight areas that i simply cannot stretch on my own.  the new pt recognizes how crucial this is, and i can attest to the importance of this.

i really like kaiser in many ways, but in terms of pt the experience has been literally painful.  i've asked permission for an outside pt referral but if you're familiar with kaiser you understand how almost impossible that is.  this is a shame because i've probably cost them more money in terms of constant doctor appointments, mris, x-rays, etc. than what they could have paid for an outside pt for a few months. i could only afford to pay out of pocket for just a few sessions so i now spend hours each day doing self pt at home.  the personal cost of being in pain is enormous  - financially, emotionally, and socially.  i truly wish that an excellent organization like kaiser, which seems to genuinely care about public health, would take another approach to their treatment of physical therapy and pain management.

i was transferred to john muir inpatient from contra costa regional medical center's psychiatric emergency services (ccrmc, pes) located in martinez. john muir was definitely an upgrade, but i suppose anything would be better than pes.

i had 2 inpatient stays, both in february 2020. the first was from february 6 to february 10. the second was from february 18 to february 26. the first discharge was premature, but the second one was helpful in my recovery.

i was admitted on the second day of my 5150 (72 hour hold) as i had attempted suicide. the remainder of the stay was on a voluntary basis as i was willing to comply with treatment. the oak adult unit has friendly staff. most of them aren't licensed therapists, but they are still knowledgeable in various therapy concepts. i really enjoyed the groups, especially expressive arts. the registered nurses are professional and check in with you frequently to make sure you are safe. 

the psychiatrist i worked with, dr. mundi, is a jerk. when i shared what had pushed me to hurt myself, he was very dismissive. i made sure to let the staff know, and was assigned to a nurse practitioner during my second inpatient stay.

the food is really good. they really care about their patients health, both physical and mental. we had patio breaks throughout the day which was our only time to get fresh air. the nurses giving medication were very nice and helped me understand the specifics such as side effects and a time frame to notice improved mood.

naturally, i was home sick, but we were allowed to have visitors and access to a phone to call our family. the rooms had 2 beds, and a bathroom with a shower. 

the reason i was admitted again was because the first discharge was premature. the post discharge care plan did not work, and no one followed up with me despite me leaving several voicemails. fortunately, the second time around the post discharge care plan worked great and i was able to get a referral for further care at a crisis residental, hope house in martinez.

i give john muir behavioral health 4 stars. the facilty was clean, the staff was nice, the rooms were safe, and the food was good. there were rounds conducted every 15 minutes to make sure everyone was accounted for. it may affect your sleep, but the staff tries to be very quiet. safety is very important, so it didn't bother me.

on a side note, my very first inpatient stay was at fremont hospital in 2018. though the facilty was bigger and had a pool and court, i felt the staff was very impersonal. john muir behavioral health may not have all the extra features fremont hospital has, but quality is better than quantity. you are seen as a person, not as your diagnosis.

i went to the emergency room complaining of an increased heart rate, the onset of significant fatigue, nausea, and vague pain in my feet.  i was confused and thinking slowly. i told them these symptoms started a couple of days ago one night after work when i was trying to go to sleep. i thought i was having a bout of tachycardia as i had been diagnosed with svt in the past.

i was given an ekg, a chest x-ray, and two blood tests. on the way to get my chest x-ray, the technician was taking me back to the x-ray room and i suffered a severe abdominal cramp. after that subsided, i was taken back into the waiting room until a room had been prepared for me. once in the room, a pa came in and gave me a medical examination. i had to sit up in bed so that she could listen to my lungs. when i sat up, i again had a severe abdominal cramp. she immediately stopped the examination and said she was going to order fluids.

an iv catheter was inserted into my arm but the fluids the pa supposedly ordered never came. i laid on the bed clutching my stomach, trying my best not to move as i felt like any movement might set off another spasm.

eventually dr. zachary simms came in with the pa in tow. this was the first time i had seen or spoken to him at all the entire night. he immediately told me that i was having a panic attack and that my symptoms were psychosomatic. the basis of this diagnosis was that outside of the ekg, the other tests had come back normal, combined with a distant (about 10 years or so) diagnosis of generalized anxiety disorder. i told him i didn't think this was a panic attack, as i am familiar with how a panic attack feels. his response was a speech about how i was going to be in and out of emergency rooms for my entire life, i was always going to feel bad, and that i needed to go see a psychiatrist. he gave me a prescription for vistaril. he was explaining what the medication was, when i told him that i had taken vistaril before and was familiar with it. his response was condescending and something along the lines of "yes, i'm sure you have." i told him i wasn't there for pills, especially anxiety medications as i try to only take them when i feel they are absolutely necessary. i again tried to explain that i hadn't really felt anxiety in a while, which was met with further indifference. he told me one day i was going to have a real medical emergency and i wouldn't get help because of my panic attacks. it was one of those classic "if you weren't crazy, you'd agree with me that you're crazy" catch-22s.

he eventually just left and i was told to leave. despite still feeling pretty horrible, i did so, mostly because i didn't have the energy to get into some prolonged argument. i was provided with zero assistance. i slowly drove myself back to my house and, being exhausted, immediately went to sleep.

the next day i woke up with a severe headache, dry mouth, cramping, a racing heart, and nausea. i sat down in the bathroom and tried to take some tylenol, which caused me to begin dry retching. following dr. simms' advice that my symptoms were induced with anxiety, i powered through it and went to work at my job as a carpenter. i sipped water throughout the day as much as i could, but my symptoms just got worse. eventually i said to hell with it and decided to ignore dr. simms' diagnosis.

i realized i hadn't urinated in about two days at that point, and when i did, my urine was a deep yellow/brownish color and low in volume. it turns out a combination of a new diet, the recent heat, and the vigorous nature of my job had put me in a state of dehydration. after fluid replacement, my symptoms began to subside.

so to summarize, a man who works outside in the sun all day doing physical labor came into the er after work, complaining of an increased heart rate, fatigue, pain, and more or less just feeling like crap. he had a history of increased heart rate and a distant history of anxiety and depression. while in the er, he suffered two massive cramps. rather than going to the very simple conclusion of dehydration, dr. simms', who i can only assume at this point is the disowned love-child of carl jung and christian bernard, decided that i was deluded and suffering from a complex reaction to anxiety. i also can only assume that he told the pa to not give me any fluids, though i will be attempting to find out whether or not that is true monday evening.

unfortunately, as far as i understand it, this is not a case of malpractice; not because of how dr. simms' decided to handle this issue, but because i did not suffer any significant injury as a direct result of it. i will be following up with a complaint to the hospital and any relevant governing bodies that i can find, as well as posting this review anywhere that is applicable. i doubt anything will come of it, but it will at least give me a sense of vindication.

doc_text:
my partner ross died in huntington hospital after waiting a week for an operation when dr. tiner, the oral surgeon the hospital provided, would not accept his dental or medical insurance and insisted on payment in advance first. this was after ross was admitted to the hospital via the er  and diagnosed with endocarditis from a strep infection. ross told dr. cohen, his heart surgeon, about dr. tiner but dr. cohen defended dr. tiner, saying he had spoken to him in the past, and he was the only one the hospital uses, and he's a "fine surgeon." nothing more came of that. 

i found out later that the "oral surgeon" the hospital had provided wasn't actually a licensed oral surgeon or dentist; he was a plastic surgeon, and the hospital did not provide anyone else after ross complained about it to dr. cohen. i tried twice to pay for it with a credit card. dr. tiner scheduled the surgery but when the first credit card declined the charge, he canceled the surgery until i offered a different credit card. by the time that was approved, ross had a stroke, and now neither surgery could be done. he was put on life support.

dr. cohen told me if it were up to him, he would stop treatment now because it was "very costly and risky" and the odds of survival were slim. i wouldn't approve of that yet since nothing had been done, and if there were any chance at all, no matter how slim, i would give ross a chance at life. i thought that was what doctors do, that's what hospitals are for. so the very next day, guess what happened...?  dr. tiner showed up and he finally pulled ross' teeth, even though he was now on a ventilator and on life support, in far worse condition than he had been the prior week. that took slightly more than an hour.

what was the medical reason for why that couldn't have been done ten days earlier, when ross was not on life support? why did huntington hospital allow a doctor to wait so long when they knew this was a serious, life threatening infection? and why did they bring in a plastic surgeon when he needed a dentist, preferably one who can bill a dental insurance plan?

i must have asked those questions a dozen times to different people between march 5 and march 15, but i never got a consistent answer. every time i asked, i either got an evasion or a change of subject. nobody gave a medical reason for making ross wait a week or why payment in advance came before saving someone's life. in fact, dr. enriquez from palliative care told me this was "standard procedure;" those were her exact words. ross never came off life support and he died in that coma on march 15. at least he was spared knowing. 

so if you take a loved one to huntington hospital's er and he gets admitted because he needs an operation to save his life, i recommend the following:

1. make sure the doctor they provide is licensed to do it first, don't assume it;
2. bring extra cash in case he isn't licensed and therefore can't take your insurance;
3. don't waste your breath complaining if he insists on being paid first, it won't do you any good; 
4. if you pay out of pocket, make sure you get a receipt before he dies.

i've been trying to get the records for ross' treatment so that the insurance company will reimburse me for my credit card, but the hospital refuses to give me any proof that they performed an operation that i paid for. i could have used that money to give ross a decent funeral and burial. just think - if i had taken him to a different hospital, i might not even have had to bury him at all.

want to hear a real kicker? the mortuary cost less than the surgery, and they even gave me the paperwork to prove it. nothing to hide there. 

my advice: go to any other hospital if you can. the staff and nurses and junior doctors were all great, but the two lead doctors? i don't know what they were thinking, i can't imagine what they were thinking, or how they sleep at night. i wonder how they'd like it if this happened to one of their family members. all i know is they didn't do anything until it was too late, and since nobody wants to answer my questions, i'm left to come to my own conclusions: one thought his money was more important than ross' life, and the other was content to not do anything about that even after the patient asked, and palliative care said that's "standard procedure."  i don't know if she meant standard for the entire industry, or only for huntington hospital, or just those two doctors; that part wasn't clear. 

this wasn't a medical mistake; it was a financial decision. if someone from the hospital can explain it another way and in person, i'm willing to listen. but i want answers to specific questions, no deflections, evasions or tap dancing acts. 

otherwise, if you can afford first class insurance, huntington probably pays attention to you, but if you can only afford third class, good luck finding your way to the lifeboats.

doc_text:
my wife and i have been to this hospital twice, once when our daughter was born in 2016 and again when our son was born in 2020.

in 2016 i would describe our experience as average.  we had some good nurses and some pretty lousy ones, the doctor was fantastic, the food service employees were rude and awful.  altogether a pretty middling experience.

when we returned in 2020, it was clear that a lot of changes had been made.  every nurse we had, day and night, was incredibly friendly and helpful.  my wife, who is very introverted and has trouble with new people, took to them immediately.  in particular she absolutely loved our night nurse in postpartum, anny.  the delivery nurse, nicole, was also outstanding - she didn't leave our room for the final 4-6 hours of labor and basically acted as a midwife.

the room service staff was also excellent; they made sure that both of us were well-fed during our time there, and were very polite on the phone.  food was delivered promptly, they would call the room around meal times if we forgot to do so, and the food was pretty good - you certainly wouldn't come here to eat if you weren't in the hospital, but it's much better than you would expect from hospital food.  lots of healthy options, and the fruit tray is clearly fresh fruit and not canned.

we were visited by multiple doctors, pediatricians, nurse practitioners, and the hospital's lactation specialist, who were all very patient and professional and spent significantly more time with us than i expected - they didn't leave the room until they had answered every question we had.  we never felt like we were rushed so they could go to the next room.

the facilities were great.  the delivery room itself was comfortable for both of us, and it's clear that improvements have been made to the postpartum room because it was also much more comfortable, including a better sleeping space for dads / partners.  it used to be a chair that did not recline, now it is a chair that folds out into a makeshift bed.  you could do much worse spending the night in the hospital.  also of importance to dads / partners - the wifi is very good.

excellent care was taken of my wife and child; although we don't plan to have more children, we would still recommend this hospital for medical needs.  it is also clear that the hospital takes feedback very seriously - we were asked by the heads of basically every department if we had any criticisms or areas of improvement, and several of them mentioned that they had been making some changes in the last couple of years to make patients and guests more comfortable and happy.

after our 2016 visit we weren't impressed, and the only reason we came back in 2020 is because my wife loved her doctor and nurse so much and wanted to deliver with them again.  i'm so glad we did come back though - it was a completely different and completely wonderful experience for all three of us.

well, it has been just under 4 years since i was admitted here as a patient. it is still uncomfortable to remember and discuss this time in my life which triggered the most massive upheaval of my life, i've experienced to this day. i stayed here twice in less than one year. 

     one lesson i have learned by being admitted to a mental health facility is that the brain is a delicate, fragile part of you and what happened to me could happen to any person at any time; that's the concerning part.

     i've decided to go into a little more detail about what i experienced because i believe it will help even just one person; maybe even the family and support system for a person staying here. there is no shame in living with a mental health condition. try not to let the stigma get you down. did you know having depression and or anxiety is a mental health condition? many don't but it is a fact. 

     i've always been an upstanding member of society and kept to the laws in place; i was a functioning member of society and consciously and pleasantly aware of that fact. in the winter of 2016, i suffered a psychiatric breakdown. it's quite common you know. one common culprit is stress; severe ongoing stress. i without my awareness slipped away from reality and entered the land of the lost. a very scary and uncomfortable place to be.

     i was under an immense amount of stress due to personal situations, relationships and events that occurred suddenly. i had filed for divorce and was making the necessary arrangements transitioning into that next phase of my life when it occurred.

     one minute i am me as i've known myself to be for over 40 years and from that place of comfort i lost all touch with reality. no fun. i do have some memories of this psychiatric hospital as it's common to not be able to recall memories when one experiences what i have. with time some memories are returning. i do recall not arguing nor fighting with any of the fellow patients here nor staff. this hospital is a locked facility.

     i also recall some areas that need attention: the restrooms in each patient room need work.  the shower heads? nope there aren't many of them so the water sprays all over the place. a nice pair of shoes would have been wonderful for me to wear as you have to walk around in socks on the dense linoleum floors. staff will remove the laces in shoes brought for patients, same with hooded sweatshirts and sweat pants. 

     you have to make your own bed which is excellent. and they give you clean linens to do so. the meals were good & you get 3 a day; plus snacks. once they know your not a threat to anyone or yourself and have been behaving yourself, you are given the option to leave the ward in a organized group with fellow patients and a professional leading; and head down via elevator to the the cafeteria and dine. another experience is the gymnasium. if your on your best behavior you may be asked if you'd like to go to the gymnasium and play basketball and other indoor sports. sometimes i went and other times i abstained. there is a phone for patients in the hallway and it works which is helpful. 

     not one employee here treated me unkindly. when i asked for something my request was granted if at all possible. the mental health technicians were very kind and friendly to me as well. i appreciate this even now nearly 4 years later. i feel this hospital is a safe place for anyone experiencing acute as well as chronic mental health conditions and/or complications, even if they have not been diagnosed yet. the rooms are kept clean but just to be fair, its important to understand that this is a psychiatric hospital therefore the patients who are occupying the rooms commonly are not cognitively healthy at that time so it is expected that they may elicit (just like me) odd, strange, bizarre behaviors preventing them from up-keeping their room.  

     in closing, one piece of lived-experience i will share is the mind is a very delicate creation and does not like stress. give it enough and any one persons brain chemistry can change (happened to me), altering your behavior. what i lacked during this experience was a supportive, loving, caring, intelligent empathetic spouse to help me through this unexpected and horrifically frightening experience. i hope for anyone that may experience this or something psychologically unusual for you that you have a great family and/or friend support system. i found mine once i received the necessary treatment and was able to return to my healthy cognitive self; but it took time. this hospital kept me safe during both stays here; and that's what i needed.

    if a person winds up here you/they may not be healthy cognitively at the time. maybe choose to view the situation this way verses the alternative which is they could be ill living on the street. i met homeless persons here too; they were really nice.  sierra vista is a much safer therapeutic option than what is listed above.

doc_text:
nothing strikes more fear in all of us during this era of covid-19 (well, except for the virus itself), than the thought of a trip to the er.

under normal conditions, an er visit is very stressful, but in the era of covid-19, it's incapacitating.

yet, here i found myself on a monday morning after experiencing lightning streaks coming out of my left eye all weekend. it was mystifying and scary. 

a quick trip to dr. google led me to a possible diagnosis, a detached retina, and these words, " seek medical help immediately." 

i live smack dab in the middle between two ers. i found out the hard way, that while one will offer a slick, state of the art environment, you will encounter indifferent, uncaring staff and wait times up to 8 hours.

the other er features a setting reminiscent of the tv series, m*a*s*h, all due to ongoing construction of brand new facilities.

i chose the latter. why? 

because a previous visit 18 months earlier showed a well-oiled machine, despite er patients lying on gurneys in hallways. the staff were attentive, nurturing, and very efficient.

this er, providence cedars-sinai tarzana medical center, proves that it's not the setting that matters. it's the staff!

and this is where tarzana er excels. from the friendly check-in to triage to the er doc, everyone was top-notch.

especially the doc. 

i'm a veteran of many er visits, so i know an exceptional er doc when i see one, as in the case of dr. gregory scott brewster. 

i have not met a more compassionate, attentive, sympathetic and driven er doc. ever.

he goes far beyond what is required. i listened for two hours as he not only took care of at least a dozen patients, but chased down specialists and patients' personal mds on the phone. 

in my case, it took him 2 hours to find an ophthalmologist willing to see me. yet he never gave up.

even when he finally found one only to have the cell phone call dropped, he persevered. and found me the best retina specialist i could possibly get. 

and if that's not enough, dr. brewster followed up later with a call to see how my visit went!!! 

i am stunned and incredibly grateful that such a professional exists.

and it says a lot about the organization which hires him.

i agree with both reviews of janny k and tina k. i am giving one star for there were times, not many, that i could speak into my father's ear over the phone- briefly. my father passed away due to their negligence!! families need to be with their loved one's during recovering; 1 for advocacy and the other for support and love!! my father, prior to being transferred here from icu, was alert and fully cognizant.  he just needed long term recovery for he still required a ventilator and had a trach and g-tube. please keep in mind that this occurred during the covid-19 epidemic, therefore, visitation was not allowed. this was very difficult for us and the only updates that we could get were via telephone. as far as zoom/face time, the client advocate informed me that unfortunately we could only see my father 2x per week via zoom for only 10 to 15min. there was not enough man power to see your loved one daily.  this was not so pleasing to our ear but 2x was better then none. i unfortunately never got to see my father for our face time appointment; he passed away prior to the first scheduled zoom meeting. 
the first morning and afternoon of admittance, everything seemed normal as far as updates. however, the first alarming news was when i spoke to the case manager who stated that my father was not responding. my father was responding and following commands/nodding yes or no to questions prior to the transfer.  also, the case manager stated that he had an occupational therapy evaluation and that he was not following simple commands. this was also alarming, for prior to that day he was receiving physical therapy at icu and following commands. the day shift nurse that day did me the favor of placing me in my father's ear via telephone so that he can hear my voice. however, the night shift nurse stated that they were too busy. this particular nurse mentioned that he had 9 patients during his shift; 9 patients? how can one nurse be in charge of 9 patients? are patients being constantly moved and cleaned?  every time i would call to speak to someone, it seemed as though they were overwhelm or too busy. we received contradicting information as well. the following day, i inquired about the medication/antibiotics that my father was receiving and the day shift nurse stated that he was not receiving any- what? he had pneumonia- why was he not receiving the antibiotics that were administered to him? she stated that my father's white blood counts were okay and he was fighting a fever therefore he did not have an infection- what?? if your body has a fever, your body is fighting an infection! she informed me that my father was only being administered tylenol for the fever. i called the house supervisor immediately and asked to speak to the doctor in charge. the house supervisor seemed overwhelmed as well when i spoke to her. she indicated that if she had time, she would do her best to call the doctor and inform him. i never spoke with the doctor. i called the number that they provided and never heard from him. i called the night shift nurse that day and he stated that he was receiving antibiotics. i asked, " which one is it- either he is receiving or not"? what was there plan of care for my father?  the following day my father passed away. we live about 86 miles away from baldwin park, therefore when we arrived, my father was already deceased. the doctor was not present when we arrived and we demanded for him to come back and speak to us as to what occurred. the doctor did finally return and sat with my family and i, alongside with the head nurse and house supervisor. the  doctor used the term "supposedly" my father threw up and they stopped administering food to him. " supposedly"- what really occurred? the doctor looked at the staff nurse and supervisor when informing us of the incident-as though trying to make sure that they were on the same page. 
conclusion- my father did not receive the proper care that he needed here. he needed constant care for his vent settings as well as for his trach and g-tube. when we walked in to see my father's body, the staff kept to themselves as though scared to speak to us. as we walked the hallways, many of the patients looked as though they were already near death. i deeply regret sending my father here. the room in which my father was in, was not what we expected. there was no chart on the walls explaining who was the nurse, etc. the family pictures, that we asked the nurses to place on his wall, were not displayed. they were tucked away/shoved away in the closet. the room, although shared with two other patients, felt lonely. my brother mentioned as he was mourning my father's dead body that day( they only allowed two family members at a time), that a staff member walked in to ask," where are they taking his body." seriously- we just received the news that my father passed and you see us mourning his body- no empathy here ! please do not send your loved one here!

overall my experiences at scripps encinitas have been relatively positive for having to stay in the hospital. i've also stayed at scripps encinitas about 6 times over the last 3 years, so i know how the process works, and knowing what to expect is helpful. 

positives:
1. treated quickly (this has to do with the condition i have), unfortunately, if you have a broken arm, just like most hospitals, it will probably take longer to be treated.
2. er is a major improvement from 10 years ago, private rooms with doors.
3. good experience with every doctor i've had.
4. i've only had to share a room 2 out of 7 times, however this also had to do with my condition. 
5. they allowed my boyfriend/fiance/and now husband to stay overnight with me when i was in my own room.
6. 90%+ of nurses i've had here have been helpful and sweet.
7. the billing process has significantly improved through online portal.
8. access to medical records and tests as well as communication online is helpful.
9. pcu and the standard hospital rooms on that floor are very nice. 

possible negatives:
1. possibility of not having a private room. this is huge for me. if you are sick, in pain, and recovering, you want your own space and a space for someone to stay with you. all new hospitals in the san diego area are required to have their own rooms now, i'm sure they will get there and understand it's a big undertaking, but it makes a big difference for experience and patient care. 
2. nurse response time - this can be long (i never experienced longer than 20-30 minutes at any given time), and i understand that there are tons of other patients to care for, however, if you are not allowed to get up to go to the bathroom by yourself or your pain really spikes 20-30 minutes can seem like forever. overall, the response time was adequate. 
3. lack of communication between doctors & nurses. i felt like i had to advocate and/or repeat for myself on several occasions. maybe notes weren't written down, maybe doctors don't always read them, who knows. my surgeon also has privileges at this hospital but is not based out of scripps encinitas, so there may be some gaps due to that.
4. not all of the hospital is updated. some floors and areas are, but some feel pretty old.

after my friend fell in january of 2019 and was not found for over three days, she was in dire physical condition and required a tracheostomy to stop recurring pneumonia infections. once stabilized, she was moved to barlow respiratory hospital, one of the best facilities of its kind in the country. here she had the medical and physiotherapy attention she required as well as a staff willing to take the time to understand her.

eventually, all her determination could not will her body back to health and it finally gave out but, to the end, she appreciated the doctors and staff at barlow who took care of her physical challenges and made her life worth more than just existing and, especially, those who enjoyed her twisted sense of humor.

if i could rate this place zero stars i would, the visit was a nightmare from start to finish. i came in to the er on a weekend with agonizing abdominal pain. i'd heard the horror stories about this place but i was very new to the area and was in such intense pain that i just wanted to get the closest care possible. i was triaged and put in a waiting room where i was left to sit in pain for an hour and a half. then finally, i was brought back to what i thought would finally be my room, but i was just placed in another waiting room where i sat for another 30 minutes. i appreciate that there is a lot going on behind the scenes that contributes to long wait times in the er, but this hospital was seemingly empty, with staff just standing around talking. 

finally i get brought back to a room and see the doctor (oluwaseye acabi). nobody asked me for a list of medications i was currently on or for any sort of medical history. i explain to him that i was having severe abdominal pain and that i had an iud and a history of bad ovarian cysts. i told him that i was afraid that either my iud had migrated or i had a cyst that was causing my ovary to twist (which would need to be treated immediately if that were the case). he proceeded to tell me that the iud migrating would be impossible after having it in for a year already. 

he then asked me if i wanted a pelvic exam and/or an ultrasound, which i thought was odd considering he was supposed to be the expert and should know what he needs to do to figure out and solve the problem. i said yes to both. he started the pelvic exam and it was by far the weirdest and most uncomfortable pelvic exam i have ever had. it was clear that he didn't know what he was doing, but i'll leave out the graphic details. 

he then tells me that i am welcome to wait for an ultrasound but that i "wasn't a priority" and would be waiting all night. at this point i was so fed up, tired, and in so much pain that i just wanted to go home and get in bed, there were no beds in the rooms for me to try and get comfortable in while i waited, so i told them to discharge me. 

they came in with the discharge papers and they'd given me bs diagnoses of pelvic inflammatory disease and dehydration. he also prescribed me antibiotics (which i didn't take because i had a feeling i didn't need them, and my obgyn confirmed), and muscle relaxers. mind you, they never took down my medications so they would have never known if i had any medicines that would interact. 

as i'm being discharged, he comes in and tells me "oh by the way, during your pelvic, i couldn't find the strings to your iud. i didn't look any further because i didn't want to inconvenience you." i am still confused as to how he would have "inconvenienced me" by doing his job and investigating the problem that brought me to him in the first place. 

so i went home and stayed in extreme pain until i could get in with my obgyn. within seconds, my ultrasound tech was able to tell me that my iud was embedded in the wall of my uterus and needed to be taken out (something the er doctor told me was impossible, if you remember). when my doctor came in she did a pelvic and was instantly able to see my iud strings clear as day... the ones the er doctor claimed he couldn't find. 

i've been to a lot of bad doctors and hospitals and had a lot of bad experiences but this one takes the cake. i paid $500 to wait around in pain and to be treated with extreme negligence and incompetence. stay far away.

during covid-19, right after the travel ban, i was on quarantine for 14 days since i arrived from europe on vacation.  during that time, i fell ill and after a few days under virtual care, my doctor advised me to go to the er.  i chose memorial hermann sugar land thinking i would get good care.  i was totally wrong.

once in the er, which was set up efficiently because of the virus, the er doctor immediately explained to me that they will not send my covid-19 test off to be tested unless i was admitted to the hospital.  his main concern was not diagnosing my problem but explaining that i would have to go somewhere else to get tested for covid-19.

i was advised to go the the er by my doctor because i was coughing excessively, barely able to breath, experiencing pain in my back when breathing and coughing, wheezing and extreme shortness of breath even with using an inhaler.  my temp stayed below 100.4 so it wasn't considered a fever.

the er began to run tests:  chest x-rays, ct scan, urine-analysis, blood-work, i.v., etc.

i waited about 45 minutes for all the test results to return and during that time, i suffered and tried to breath over and over in spite of the difficulties i was experiencing.  finally, the er doctor returned (dr. b. parker) and said that my lungs were clear and that the covid-19 swab would not be sent to the lab because i'm not being admitted to the hospital.  i stated that i understood about the swab but i didn't understand what was going on with my breathing so i asked him again about my lungs.  dr. parker repeated that my lungs were "all clear" and that there was no sign of the virus in my lungs. 

i asked the doctor what was he diagnosing me as having. since we know there's no sign of covid-19 in my lungs, what is it then and what was he going to give me to help me breath.   dr. parker turned the paper around and it read, "cough - adult".  i asked, "so you're diagnosing me as having a cough?"  he replied yes.  i was dumbfounded.  i came to the er with a cough and shortness of breath and now the dr. was telling me that i had a cough.  wow!  

i asked him what was he going to do about helping me?  he stated that he was calling in prescriptions to my pharmacy to take but to act like i had covid-10 and still isolate.  he stated that he believed it was just an allergy infection and that these meds would clear it up.  i informed him that i don't typically suffer with allergies and that i had been taking zyrtec because the virtual doctor i spoke to recommended it but i wasn't getting any better.  he reemphasized again that the test would not be sent and that if i wanted a covid-19 test, i needed to go to another site.  i asked about an antibiotic to clear up the infection and he said the meds he prescribed would clear up the infection.  i later learned that the meds were regular over-the-counter stuff that i had already been using that wasn't effective:  tylenol, mucinex and claritin-d.

i believe dr. parker's only concern was covid-19 and not finding the real source of my problems.  i asked my discharge nurse again about my lungs being "all clear" and she said well they are not all clear and that they had a haze over them.  i asked what does a haze mean.  she informed me that the doctor believes the haze is possibly from a bacteria infection from allergies so he's prescribed some meds to help.  i again said i don't suffer with allergies but ok the pollen is high so i guess.  

i was discharged and walked to my car still struggling to breath just the same way as i walked into the hospital.   

that was saturday, march 21st. fast forward to wednesday, march 25th and i was not feeling any better, in fact, i felt worse. i called my doctor both the 25th and 26th and left messages. her nurse called my back on the 27th and informed me to stop taking all allergy meds immediately and that she had reviewed the labs and x-rays and they believe that haze over my right lung is pneumonia.

pneumonia?!!  so i had pneumonia in the right lung for an additional 6 days without any treatment?!  why would dr. parker say i was "all clear" and ignore the haze?  i had to take additional time from work to heal whereas if dr. parker would have just taken the time to explore my results for something more than covid-19, he could have treated me correctly and i could have returned back to work without taking additional time.  

lastly, once i got the bill, i saw that i was billed $273.50 for a pregnancy test!!!  the admitting nurse asked if there was anyway i could be pregnant, i immediately answered no and explained why i couldn't be.  so why would you give me, a 49 yr old woman with a valid reason a pregnancy test?  especially for $273.50.  over billing???   yes!

i will never go back to memorial hermann sugar land emergency room.  the care of the treating physician was below sub-par and i could have saved way more time and money going to another facility.
